section: Cost and Efficiency: The Economics of Storage
hook: Shut down a server and its bill disappears. Stop using a dataset and the bill keeps coming. Why?
title: Storage is the bill that grows while you sleep
body: Most tech costs stop when you stop using them. Turn off a server and its compute charge disappears. Data is different. The bytes you stop using stay on disk, and you pay for them every month until someone deletes them. That makes every stored byte a **recurring liability**, and storage cost only goes up by itself. At exabyte scale, a 10% efficiency gain is worth tens of millions of dollars per year.
takeaway: Compute you forget about stops billing. Data you forget about bills forever.
deeper:
**Why papers chase money:** The largest storage papers, Meta's f4 and Tectonic and Azure's Local Reconstruction Codes, are as much about money as about engineering. Shaving a fraction of overhead off exabytes turns straight into savings.

**Small choices compound:** How many copies to keep, which drive to buy, whether to set an expiry date. Each looks minor at design time. Each is then paid every month, for years, on every byte it touches.

**Where the money hides:** The drive price is one line of a much longer bill. Redundancy, fill headroom, servers, power, requests, egress and people all multiply or add to it. The levers that cut it fall into two groups: store fewer bytes, or pay less per byte.

**The catch:** Deleting takes a decision. Keeping takes none. Without an owner and a default expiry, forgotten data never leaves.

quiz.q: A team shuts down a batch cluster but keeps its 2 PB of output "just in case". What happens to each part of their bill over the next year?
quiz.a: Compute cost drops to zero at once. The storage charge stays and is billed every month, because data you stop using stays stored until someone deletes it.

mcq.q: Why does storage cost tend to rise on its own while compute cost does not?
options: Unused data stays stored and billed until someone deletes it
Storage prices per GB rise every year with inflation
Cloud providers charge more for data as it gets older
Compute is billed only while it is under heavy load
mcq.why: Compute you stop using goes away. Data you stop using stays, and you keep paying for it every month.

hook: A hard drive costs about $15 per TB. So why does a served terabyte cost far more?
title: A $15 drive is one line of a six-line bill
body: Quote a drive at $15 per TB and you have priced one line of the bill. A usable, durable, served terabyte has six parts: media, servers (chassis, CPU, RAM, network cards), redundancy overhead, power and cooling, datacenter space and network, and people and software. The full number is **total cost of ownership (TCO)**: the cost of owning and operating something over its whole life, not just its purchase price.
takeaway: The drive price is the sticker. TCO is the bill.
deeper:
**How each line behaves:** Media is the drives. Server cost is shared across the drives in each machine, so density matters. Redundancy multiplies both: 3× replication triples media and server cost, while erasure coding cuts the multiplier to about 1.3× to 1.7×.

**The recurring lines:** Power and cooling are paid every hour for drives, CPUs and fans, with cooling on top. Space and network cover racks, floor space, top-of-rack switches and the bandwidth to read data back. People and software cover engineers, on-call, hardware replacement and licenses.

**The catch:** A design with cheaper drives can still cost more if it needs more copies, more servers or more operators. The drive line is simply the easiest one to see.

**Use it:** List all six lines, even as rough estimates, before calling one option cheaper than another.

quiz.q: Option A uses $12/TB drives with 3× replication. Option B uses $15/TB drives with erasure coding at 1.4×. A manager picks A because its drives are cheaper. What is wrong?
quiz.a: Redundancy multiplies media and server cost. A's media alone costs about $36 per usable TB versus about $21 for B, before servers, power and people are even counted.

mcq.q: Which set lists the six parts of storage TCO?
options: Media, servers, redundancy, power and cooling, space and network, people and software
Media, servers, redundancy, requests, egress, and retrieval fees
Media, controllers, RAID cards, backups, snapshots, and licenses
Media, power, cooling, CDN, cross-zone transfer, and support contracts
mcq.why: TCO counts what it costs to own and run a usable, durable, served TB. Requests and egress are cloud bill lines, not ownership costs.

hook: Backblaze's hard drive cost fell from $0.114 to $0.014 per GB. Why doesn't that make storage cheap?
title: Disk cost per GB fell about 8× from 2009 to 2022

stat.label: per GB for 16 TB drives, Backblaze, late 2022

body: Few companies publish what they pay for drives. **Backblaze** does. It reported about $0.014 per GB (about $14 per TB) for 16 TB drives in late 2022, down from $0.114 per GB in 2009. That fall made raw disk look almost free. Yet media is a minority of the cost of a usable terabyte. Servers, redundancy, fill headroom, power, space and people now dominate.
takeaway: When the drive gets cheap, everything around it becomes the bill.
deeper:
**Why Backblaze matters:** Most big companies treat hardware pricing as secret. A public series from 2009 to 2022 shows the long-run trend: roughly an eightfold drop per GB in about thirteen years.

**Why the total moves less:** Every other line of TCO multiplies or adds to media. Redundancy multiplies it, fill headroom multiplies it, and power, space, network and people sit on top. Media is now a minority of a usable terabyte's cost, so even a big drop in drive price moves the total much less.

**Flash is a different trade:** Flash costs several times more per TB than HDD but delivers orders of magnitude more IOPS per TB. The cheapest medium per TB is not always the cheapest medium for the workload.

**The catch:** A team that cuts cost by shopping for cheaper drives is working on the smallest line.

quiz.q: Your CFO reads that disk cost per GB fell eightfold since 2009 and asks why your storage budget hasn't shrunk eightfold. What do you say?
quiz.a: Media is now a minority of TCO. Servers, redundancy, fill headroom, power, space, network and people make up most of the cost, so cheaper drives move the total far less.

mcq.q: Backblaze's figures show HDD cost per GB fell about eightfold. What does that imply for storage TCO?
options: Media is now a minority, so other lines dominate
Total storage cost fell by about the same factor
Flash is now cheaper per TB than hard disks
Redundancy overhead no longer affects the bill
mcq.why: Redundancy, servers, fill headroom, power, space and people multiply or add to media, so they now dominate cost.

hook: Dropbox kept the same CPU and memory in each storage server and still cut cost per TB. What changed?
title: Dropbox went from 60 to 100 disks per server, same CPU
body: A drive can't work alone. It needs a chassis, CPU, memory and network cards, and that server cost is shared across every drive in the box. Dropbox's 2018 SMR design went from 60 to 100 disks per machine with the same CPU and memory. The **server share** of each terabyte fell, because the same compute now fed far more disks. Denser servers spread fixed cost over more terabytes.
takeaway: Fixed cost shrinks per unit only when you pack more units behind it.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** If the server costs about the same, at 100 drives instead of 60 each drive carries 60% of the server cost it used to, a 40% cut in server cost per drive. For warm and cold data, one CPU can keep up with many slow drives, so extra compute buys nothing.

**The limit:** More drives per server means more data behind each network card and CPU, and more to rebuild when a whole machine fails. That suits large, mostly immutable blobs like Dropbox's. A hot database with heavy random reads would saturate CPU or network long before the disks filled.

**The rest of the design:** Dropbox paired the density with SMR drives, which fit more data per drive, and an SSD cache to absorb writes. The new design saved more than 20% overall versus the previous generation.

**The catch:** Density is a win for bytes at rest, not bytes in motion.

quiz.q: A team proposes moving its hot, random-read metadata store onto 100-disk servers to copy Dropbox's savings. Why might it backfire?
quiz.a: Density pays when CPU and network sit mostly idle. A hot random-access workload saturates CPU, network or IOPS long before the disks fill, so the extra capacity goes unused.

mcq.q: Why did Dropbox's move from 60 to 100 disks per machine cut cost per TB?
options: The same CPU and memory cost was spread over more drives
The larger servers ran at higher clock speeds
Each disk needed less redundancy in a denser server
Fewer servers made the drives themselves cheaper
mcq.why: Server cost is fixed per machine, so putting 100 drives behind it instead of 60 lowers the server share of every TB.

section: 12.1.1 From raw TB to usable TB
hook: A drive costs $15 per raw TB. What does one usable TB cost, and which steps inflate it?
title: Price usable TB, not raw: $15 becomes $39.40
body: Users buy **usable capacity**, not raw. A teaching example with assumed numbers: media at $15 per raw TB. Servers add about 50%, so $22.50. Keep 20% free for growth and rebuilds, so divide by 0.8: $28.10. Multiply by erasure coding at 1.4×, like RS(10,4): $39.40 per usable TB. Spread over a 5-year life, that is about $0.66 per usable TB-month, for hardware alone.
takeaway: Multipliers compound. Price the terabyte users get, not the one you buy.
deeper:
**Why divide by fill:** A cluster can never run at 100%. It needs room for growth before new hardware lands and for rebuilding data when drives fail. At 80% full, every stored byte carries 25% extra hardware.

**Why 1.4×:** RS(10,4) splits data into 10 pieces and adds 4 parity pieces, so 14 units of disk hold 10 units of data. Redundancy is the multiplier design choices swing most: 1.4× here, 3× with replication.

**Why 60 months:** The lifetime step turns a purchase into a monthly cost. A longer life lowers the monthly figure, but older drives fail more and hold less, so lifetime is its own trade-off.

**The catch:** $0.66 is hardware only. Power, space, network and people come on top, and they often equal or exceed the hardware line.

quiz.q: A colleague prices a cluster by dividing total drive spend by total raw TB. Name two multipliers they skipped and which way each pushes the cost.
quiz.a: Fill target: running 80% full divides by 0.8, raising cost. Redundancy: 1.4× erasure coding or 3× replication multiplies it. Server share and drive lifetime also belong in the math.

mcq.q: In the raw-to-usable example, why divide by 0.8?
options: 20% is kept free for growth and rebuilds
Drives lose 20% of capacity to formatting
Erasure coding needs 20% extra for parity
Servers add 20% on top of the drive cost
mcq.why: A cluster needs headroom for growth and rebuilds, so each usable byte requires extra purchased capacity.

section: 12.1.1 From raw TB to usable TB
hook: Same drives, same servers, same fill level. One design choice more than doubles the hardware bill. Which?

predict.q: Same drives, servers and fill level. Which single choice moves hardware cost per usable TB the most?
options: Redundancy: 3× replication vs 1.4× EC
Drive vendor: a 10% cheaper drive
Drive life: 5 years instead of 4

title: 3× replication more than doubles hardware cost vs EC
body: Rerun the usable-TB math with one change: 3× replication instead of 1.4× erasure coding. Hardware cost rises from about $0.66 to about $1.40 per usable TB-month. The **redundancy choice** alone more than doubles it, because redundancy multiplies both media and servers. Then add power, space, network and people, which often equal or exceed the hardware line. Media is a minority of the cost; redundancy, fill level and lifetime multiply everything.
takeaway: A drive discount trims one line. A redundancy choice rescales the whole bill.
deeper:
**Why it ripples:** Redundancy multiplies media and servers together. Going from 3.0× to 1.4× cuts physical bytes by more than half for the same user data. A discount on drives touches only the media line.

**What stays private:** Power, space, network and staffing costs are private at every big company, so the worked example does not guess them. The structure is what transfers: they sit on top of a hardware line that redundancy has already scaled.

**Who proved it:** This is why the largest storage papers chase redundancy. Meta's f4 cut its effective replication factor from 3.6 to 2.1. Azure's LRC reached about 1.33×.

**Use it:** When someone proposes a storage design, find three numbers first: redundancy factor, fill target and assumed lifetime. They tell you more about its cost than the drive model does.

quiz.q: Your team can negotiate a 10% discount on drives, or move cold data from 3× replication to RS(10,4). Which saves more hardware cost, and why?
quiz.a: The erasure coding move. It changes the multiplier on both media and servers from 3× to 1.4×, cutting physical bytes by more than half. A drive discount trims only the media line by 10%.

mcq.q: In the worked example, what happens to hardware cost per usable TB-month when 3× replication replaces 1.4× erasure coding?
options: It rises from about $0.66 to about $1.40
It rises from about $0.66 to about $0.92
It stays flat because the drives cost the same
It rises from about $0.66 to about $3.00
mcq.why: Redundancy multiplies the whole hardware line: $0.66 × 3 / 1.4 ≈ $1.40, more than double.

section: 12.1.1 From raw TB to usable TB
hook: Two honest teams on the same hardware quote cost per TB five times apart. Neither is lying. How?
title: Four questions that expose a 5× gap in cost per TB
body: Cost per TB sounds like one number. It hides at least four assumptions. Is it **raw or usable** capacity? Which redundancy scheme? What fill level? Does it include power, space and people? Each one is a multiplier, and multipliers stack. Two teams using the same hardware can be off by 5 times from these assumptions alone. Pin them down before you compare any two storage systems.
takeaway: Before arguing whose storage is cheaper, agree on what a terabyte means.
deeper:
**How 5× happens:** Raw versus usable differs by the redundancy factor, from about 1.33× to 3× or more. A cluster run at 50% full costs 1.6 times as much per stored byte as one at 80%. Adding power, space, network and people can roughly double a hardware-only figure. Stack those and a factor of five is easy.

**A fifth question:** Drive lifetime. Amortizing hardware over three years instead of five raises the monthly cost by about two-thirds.

**Where it bites:** Comparing a cloud list price, which includes everything plus margin, against the raw price of drives. Or crediting one internal team with cheaper storage when it simply runs fuller or counts fewer copies.

**The rule:** Normalize everyone to usable, durable TB with the same scope of costs, then compare.

quiz.q: Team A reports $0.30 per TB-month and Team B reports $1.50, on identical hardware. Which four questions would likely explain the gap?
quiz.a: Raw or usable capacity? Which redundancy scheme? What fill level? Does it include power, space, network and people? Drive lifetime is a fifth.

mcq.q: A cost-per-TB quote leaves out its fill level. Why does that matter?
options: Running emptier spreads hardware over fewer stored bytes
Fuller clusters need more expensive drives
Fill level changes which redundancy scheme is used
Cloud providers bill by fill level, not bytes
mcq.why: At 50% full each stored byte carries 1.6 times the hardware it would at 80%, so fill level multiplies cost.

section: 12.2 Anatomy of a cloud storage bill
hook: Two apps store exactly the same number of gigabytes on S3. One bill is far larger. How?
title: A cloud storage bill has five lines, not one
body: Engineers price cloud storage by the gigabyte. The bill has five lines. **Storage**: GB stored per month. **Requests**: a fee per API call. Retrieval: a per-GB fee for reading cool classes. **Egress**: data leaving the region to the internet. Replication and transfer: copies to other regions and traffic between zones. Only the first line tracks size. The other four track how you use the data, and any of them can dominate.
takeaway: Only one line of the bill cares how big your data is.
deeper:
**S3 US East list prices (checked 2026):** Standard storage is $0.023 per GB-month for the first 50 TB, falling to $0.021 above 500 TB. PUT, COPY, POST and LIST cost $0.005 per 1,000; GET costs $0.0004 per 1,000.

**The access lines:** Retrieval is charged per GB for the Infrequent Access and Glacier classes, which trade a lower storage price for a fee when you read. Egress to the internet is $0.09 per GB for the first tier, with the first 10 GB per month free. Replication is billed per GB transferred, plus storage of the replica.

**The catch:** Many small writes, frequent reads from cold tiers, heavy internet serving or cross-region copies reshape the bill. A capacity spreadsheet sees none of it.

**Use it:** Model writes, reads and bytes out before you model bytes stored.

quiz.q: App A stores 1 PB of large videos streamed to the internet. App B stores 1 PB of tiny log records written constantly and rarely read. Beyond storage, which line likely dominates each?
quiz.a: A: egress, since serving data to the internet costs up to $0.09 per GB. B: requests, since billions of tiny PUTs are billed per call regardless of size.

mcq.q: Which S3 bill line depends on how much data you keep rather than how you access it?
options: Storage (per GB-month)
Requests (per API call)
Egress (per GB out)
Retrieval (per GB read)
mcq.why: Storage is billed per GB stored per month. Requests, retrieval, egress and transfer all follow access patterns.

section: 12.2 Anatomy of a cloud storage bill
hook: Your app writes a billion tiny objects to S3. The storage line is small. Why is the bill not?
title: On S3, a PUT costs 12.5× more than a GET

stat.label: S3 PUT price vs GET price, per request

body: Requests feel free. They are not. S3 charges $0.005 per 1,000 PUT, COPY, POST or LIST calls and $0.0004 per 1,000 GETs. Requests are billed per call, whatever the object size, while storage is billed per byte. So small objects mean many requests per gigabyte. Write billions of tiny objects and the **request charges** can exceed the cost of storing the data.
takeaway: Bytes are cheap. Calls are not. Tiny objects turn bytes into calls.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** One million PUTs cost $5. If each object is 1 KB, the million objects total about 1 GB, which costs about two cents a month in S3 Standard. The writes cost hundreds of times more than a month of storage. With 2 MB photos, the balance flips and storage dominates.

**The design pressure:** Fewer, larger objects. Log pipelines and lake tables batch small records into big files for this reason. Compaction does the same for streaming lake tables: it merges small files into larger ones, cutting requests and improving compression, at the cost of some write amplification.

**The catch:** LIST is priced like PUT. A job that keeps listing a large prefix to find new data runs up a request bill without writing anything.

quiz.q: A telemetry service writes each 500-byte event as its own S3 object. What happens to the bill if it batches 10,000 events per object?
quiz.a: PUT requests drop about 10,000-fold while stored bytes stay the same. Requests are billed per call, so the request line, which likely dominated, nearly vanishes.

mcq.q: Why can request charges exceed storage charges on S3?
options: Requests are billed per call regardless of object size
Requests are billed per byte transferred, like egress
Storage charges are waived for small objects
GET requests cost more than PUT requests
mcq.why: Tiny objects mean huge call counts but few bytes. At $0.005 per 1,000 PUTs, the calls can outweigh the per-GB storage charge.

section: 12.2 Anatomy of a cloud storage bill
hook: Storing a gigabyte for a month is the cheap part. Serving it once is where the bill jumps.

predict.q: Sending 1 GB from S3 to the internet once costs about as much as storing it for how long?
options: About 4 months
About 1 week
About 1 month

title: Serving a GB once costs about four months of storing it
body: **Egress** is data leaving a cloud region to the internet. S3 charges $0.09 per GB for the first tier, after 10 free GB a month. Storing that GB in S3 Standard costs about $0.023 a month. So sending it out once costs about four times more than keeping it for a month. For media-heavy apps, this line can dominate. That is why companies put a **CDN** (content delivery network) in front of object storage.
takeaway: The cheapest byte to serve is the one the CDN already has.
deeper:
**How a CDN helps:** It caches popular content at edge locations near users. Only cache misses go back to the bucket, which cuts both egress and GET requests on the storage side. The playbook rates it a large saving for media, with cache misses as the main risk.

**List is not what you pay:** Large customers negotiate volume discounts. A worked bill for a photo app assumes a blended $0.05 per GB to a third-party CDN, not the $0.09 list price.

**When egress wins:** For a video streaming service sending many petabytes a month to the internet, egress would dominate the bill instead of storage, unless a CDN or peering deal absorbs it.

**Beyond the bill:** Heavy egress to users or partners is one of the factors that favors owning infrastructure over cloud.

quiz.q: A video startup stores 500 TB and streams 5 PB a month straight from S3 to viewers. Which line dominates, and what is the standard fix?
quiz.a: Egress. At up to $0.09 per GB, 5 PB out dwarfs storing 500 TB. A CDN, or a peering deal, absorbs most reads so far less data leaves the bucket.

mcq.q: Why do companies put a CDN in front of object storage?
options: Internet egress costs far more per GB than a month of storage
Object storage cannot serve reads to browsers directly
A CDN removes the need to store more than one copy
S3 charges a monthly fee for every public object
mcq.why: Egress is about $0.09 per GB, roughly four months of Standard storage. A CDN serves most reads from cache, so less data leaves the bucket.

section: 12.2 Anatomy of a cloud storage bill
hook: S3 replicates across zones without billing you. Your own database does the same and gets billed. Why?
title: AWS bills your own cross-zone replication traffic
body: S3 copies data across **Availability Zones** (isolated locations within a region) and includes that in its price. Run your own replicated database or Kafka on VMs in three zones and the rules change: AWS bills the transfer between zones. Its architecture blog notes that traffic crossing a zone boundary typically incurs a charge, while traffic inside one zone is free. The common EC2 list rate, at the time of writing, is about $0.01 per GB in each direction.
takeaway: The provider's replication is bundled. Yours is metered.
deeper:
**Why engineers miss it:** It is not a storage line. It shows up as data transfer on the compute side of the bill, far from anyone's picture of disk cost.

**The mechanism:** A self-managed database across three zones sends every write to replicas in the other two. Each transfer is billed on both ends, about $0.01 per GB out and $0.01 per GB in. So each replicated byte costs about $0.02 per destination zone, times your write volume.

**The trade-off:** Keeping replicas in one zone avoids the charge but loses zone isolation, so one zone outage can take down the whole database. The playbook lists avoiding cross-zone chatter as a lever whose saving can exceed disk cost, with lower zone isolation as its risk.

**The catch:** Rates change. Verify current prices before you model with them.

quiz.q: You spread a Kafka cluster from one zone to three for resilience. Storage per broker doesn't change. Why does the monthly bill rise?
quiz.a: Every byte is now replicated to brokers in other zones, and AWS bills cross-zone transfer on both ends, about $0.01 per GB each way, on all of that traffic.

mcq.q: Why does a self-managed 3-zone database pay transfer charges that S3's own cross-zone replication does not?
options: S3 bundles its internal replication into its storage price
S3 compresses replicas so they cross zones for free
Databases replicate over the public internet instead
S3 keeps every copy inside a single zone
mcq.why: S3's cross-zone copies are included in its price. Traffic between your own VMs in different zones is metered, about $0.01 per GB each direction.

section: 12.2 Anatomy of a cloud storage bill
hook: A database's disks can cost less than the network bill for keeping its replicas in sync. How?
title: The forgotten line: 3-zone replication traffic
body: The mistake: designing a self-managed database across three Availability Zones and pricing only the disks. Each byte written goes to two other zones, and each transfer is billed on both ends, leaving and entering. Disk is billed on the bytes you keep. **Transfer** is billed on every byte you write, including updates and overwrites that never grow the data. For a write-heavy message store, this line can be larger than the disk cost.
takeaway: Disk bills what you keep. Replication bills what you change.
deeper:
**Why churn matters:** Disk is billed once per stored GB per month. A write-heavy workload may rewrite its data many times a month, so transfer scales with churn, not size.

**A worked number:** A messages database writing 100 TB a month, copied to 2 other zones at $0.02 round-trip per GB, adds about $4,000 a month. Small next to a photo store's $1 million storage line. Large for a database whose own disk footprint is modest.

**Mitigations:** Compress replication streams. Cut write amplification. Choose a managed service whose cross-zone replication is included in its price. Or run fewer zones where durability requirements allow.

**The rule:** Put the replication topology in the cost model on day one, not on the first invoice.

quiz.q: Two databases each hold 5 TB on disk across three zones. One rewrites its data 20 times a month, the other almost never. Why can their bills differ hugely?
quiz.a: Cross-zone transfer is billed on every byte written, to two other zones, on both ends. The high-churn database pays for about 100 TB of writes a month; the other pays almost nothing.

mcq.q: Why can cross-zone replication cost more than disk for a write-heavy self-managed database?
options: Transfer is billed on every byte written, not bytes stored
Cross-zone traffic is billed at the internet egress rate
Replicas in other zones use more expensive disks
Each zone keeps a full backup as well as the replica
mcq.why: Updates and overwrites don't grow stored size, but each is copied to two zones and billed on both ends.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
hook: A billion-user app gets 25 million photo uploads a day. How does that become 3 billion PUTs a month?
title: 25 million uploads a day become 3 billion PUTs a month
body: Every cost model starts with a **back-of-envelope**. A teaching example: a 1-billion-user app on S3 US East with 50 PB of photos and videos. It gets 25 million uploads a day, each stored in 4 sizes: 100 million PUTs a day, about 3 billion a month. At 2 MB per photo across all versions, that is 50 TB a day, about 1.5 PB of growth a month. A CDN absorbs most views, so S3 sees 3 billion GETs a day.
takeaway: Count objects, not just bytes. Every object gets billed more than once.
deeper:
**Transfer assumptions:** 2 PB a month leaves AWS for a third-party CDN at an assumed blended $0.05 per GB after discounts. All new uploads are copied to a second region for disaster recovery at an assumed $0.02 per GB. A self-managed messages database spans 3 zones: 100 TB of writes a month, each copied to 2 other zones at $0.01 per GB each direction.

**The naive start:** Everything sits in S3 Standard, the priciest of the classes used here. That is deliberate: it shows which optimization matters most.

**Why 4 sizes matter:** An original plus 3 resized versions multiplies the object count, so PUTs, and later per-object transition fees, grow fourfold even though the resized versions are small.

**The habit:** Check the multiplication yourself. 25 million × 4 = 100 million objects a day; × 30 days ≈ 3 billion.

quiz.q: Product wants to add a fifth thumbnail size to every photo. Besides extra bytes, which cost lines grow, and by roughly how much?
quiz.a: PUT requests grow by a quarter, from 100 to 125 million a day, and so do later per-object lifecycle transition fees, since both are billed per object.

mcq.q: In the worked example, why do 25 million uploads a day produce 100 million PUTs a day?
options: Each photo is stored in 4 sizes
Each photo is replicated to 4 zones
Each upload is retried about 4 times
Each photo is split into 4 erasure-coded chunks
mcq.why: Every photo is saved as the original plus 3 resized versions, so each upload is 4 objects and 4 PUTs.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
hook: A photo app's first monthly S3 bill comes to about $1.27 million. One line is most of it. Which?

predict.q: A photo app's first S3 bill is about $1.27 million. What share of it is the storage line?
options: About 83%
About 40%
About 60%

title: Storage was 83% of a $1.27 million monthly bill

stat.label: of the first month's bill was the storage line

body: Build the bill line by line, with everything in S3 Standard. 50 PB at about $0.021 per GB: $1,050,000. PUTs $15,000, GETs $36,000, CDN egress $100,000, cross-region copies $30,000, new **replica storage** about $31,500, cross-zone database traffic $4,000. Total: about $1.27 million. Storage is about 83% of it. That tells you where to look first.
takeaway: Build the bill line by line. The biggest line picks your first project.
deeper:
**Why requests are small here:** Objects average 2 MB and a CDN absorbs most reads. 3 billion PUTs at $0.005 per 1,000 plus 90 billion GETs at $0.0004 per 1,000 total about $51,000, a few percent of the bill.

**The line that grows:** Every month, 1.5 PB more lands in the disaster-recovery region. Replica storage rises by about $31,500 a month, every month, compounding. The first bill understates it; a year on, that line alone adds hundreds of thousands a month.

**A different business:** A video streaming service sending many petabytes a month to the internet would see egress dominate instead.

**The catch:** 83% is a property of this workload, not of cloud storage. Rebuild the bill for yours, line by line, before choosing what to optimize.

quiz.q: Finance sees the replica storage line at $31,500 in month one and calls it negligible. Roughly what will it be in month twelve, and why?
quiz.a: About $378,000 a month. Each month adds 1.5 PB of new uploads to region 2, so the replica storage charge grows by about $31,500 every month.

mcq.q: Why does storage dominate this worked bill rather than requests or egress?
options: 50 PB at about $0.021 per GB dwarfs the other lines
S3 waives request fees above 1 billion a month
Egress to a CDN is free of charge
The CDN also pays for the GET requests
mcq.why: At this read and write rate, request and transfer lines are small next to 50 PB billed per GB-month.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
hook: 60% of a photo store's bytes are rarely viewed but must still load instantly. Where should they live?
title: Assume 10% hot, 30% warm, 60% cold: three S3 classes
body: Photos cool within about 3 months of upload. Suppose access data for a photo store shows 10% of bytes hot, 30% warm (read about once every few months), and 60% cold but still expected to load in milliseconds when a user scrolls back. Each group can move to a cheaper S3 class. Hot stays in Standard. Warm goes to **Standard-IA**. Cold goes to **Glacier Instant Retrieval**, which still serves reads in milliseconds.
takeaway: Tier by how often data is read, and by how fast it must come back.
deeper:
**Latency sets the floor:** Cold photos are rarely viewed, but when someone scrolls back through old posts they must appear instantly. That rules out archival classes that take minutes or hours to restore. Glacier Instant Retrieval trades a much lower storage price for a per-GB retrieval fee.

**The prices:** Standard $0.021 per GB-month, Standard-IA $0.0125, Glacier Instant Retrieval $0.004. The cold class is about five times cheaper than Standard.

**Measure, don't guess:** The split must come from measured access data. Tier data that turns out to be read often and retrieval fees can wipe out the saving.

**The catch:** Access patterns drift. Measurement has to be ongoing, which is one reason access-based automatic tiering exists as its own lever. It moves objects by observed use instead of a fixed rule.

quiz.q: A team wants to move 3-year-old photos to an archive class that takes hours to restore, since almost nobody views them. Which requirement does this break?
quiz.a: Cold photos must still load in milliseconds when a user scrolls back. An hours-long restore breaks that; Glacier Instant Retrieval gives a low price with instant reads.

mcq.q: Why does the example tier cold photos to Glacier Instant Retrieval instead of a deeper archive class?
options: They must still load in milliseconds when viewed
Deeper archive classes cost more per GB-month
Instant Retrieval has no retrieval fees at all
Deeper archives cannot hold objects over 1 MB
mcq.why: Cold photos are rarely viewed but must appear instantly when a user scrolls back, so the class must serve millisecond reads.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
hook: Move a photo store's bytes to cheaper classes by how often they're read. How much of the bill goes?

predict.q: Tiering 50 PB of photos by measured access (10% hot, 30% warm, 60% cold) cuts the storage line by about:
options: More than 60%
About 15%
About 30%

title: Tiering cut the storage line by more than 60%
body: Start with 50 PB in S3 Standard at about $1.05 million a month. Move bytes by measured access: 5 PB stays in Standard ($105,000), 15 PB goes to Standard-IA ($187,500), 30 PB to Glacier Instant Retrieval ($120,000). Add about $6,000 in **retrieval fees** for an assumed 300 TB read back. The storage subtotal is about $418,500, a saving of more than 60%. The whole bill falls from about $1.27 million to about $640,000.
takeaway: Move the biggest pile of bytes to the cheapest class that still meets latency.
deeper:
**Where the money went:** The cold tier holds 60% of the bytes but costs $120,000, less than the 15 PB warm tier. The biggest win is the largest group of bytes on the cheapest class that still meets the latency need.

**The counterweight:** Retrieval fees. 300 TB a month read from IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval at about $0.01 to $0.03 per GB is around $6,000. Small, because cold data really is rarely read. A monthly scan of the whole cold tier could swamp the saving.

**Minimum durations:** An object deleted soon after moving to a cool class is still billed for the minimum period. Short-lived data should not be tiered.

**The playbook view:** Lifecycle tiering often saves more than half of storage cost for cold data, at low effort, with retrieval fees and minimum durations as the risks.

quiz.q: After tiering, an analytics team starts a monthly job that scans every cold photo to retrain a model. What happens to the saving?
quiz.a: Each scan reads 30 PB from Glacier Instant Retrieval and pays per-GB retrieval fees. At $0.01 to $0.03 per GB, that is $300,000 to $900,000 a month, erasing much or all of the saving.

mcq.q: After tiering, which class holds the most bytes, and what does it cost per month?
options: Glacier Instant Retrieval: 30 PB for about $120,000
Standard-IA: 30 PB for about $375,000
Standard: 30 PB for about $630,000
Glacier Instant Retrieval: 15 PB for about $60,000
mcq.why: 60% of 50 PB is cold. At $0.004 per GB-month, 30 PB costs about $120,000, less than the 15 PB warm tier.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
hook: Tiering 2 MB photos pays back in under a month. Tiering 20 KB thumbnails can lose money. Why?

predict.q: Tiering the same bytes as 20 KB thumbnails instead of 2 MB photos multiplies the transition cost by about:
options: 1× (no change)

title: Tiering tiny objects can cost more than it saves
body: Moving objects between classes has a hidden one-time cost: **lifecycle transitions** are billed per object. 45 PB of 2 MB photos is about 22.5 billion objects. At an assumed few cents per 1,000 transitions, moving them costs hundreds of thousands of dollars once, and pays back in under a month. Shrink objects to 20 KB thumbnails and the object count is 100 times larger. The transition cost can exceed the saving.
takeaway: Fees per object, savings per byte. Tiny objects lose that race.
deeper:
**The mismatch:** Transition fees scale with object count. Savings scale with bytes. Big objects carry many bytes per fee; tiny ones carry few. Below some size, the per-object fee outweighs years of per-byte savings.

**The built-in guard:** S3 Intelligent-Tiering and Google Cloud Storage Autoclass never tier objects under 128 KB. Access-based tiering also charges a per-object monitoring fee, another cost small objects can't justify.

**Three ways tiering rarely-read data still loses:**
1. Objects are tiny, so transition and monitoring fees beat the saving.
2. Data is deleted before the minimum storage duration.
3. Occasional full scans trigger retrieval fees larger than the saving.

**The rule:** Model object count, not just bytes, before you turn on a lifecycle rule. A bucket's byte total tells you the saving; its object count tells you the fee.

quiz.q: You have 1 PB of 10 KB JSON files that nobody reads. Why might a lifecycle rule to a colder class be a bad idea?
quiz.a: 1 PB of 10 KB files is about 100 billion objects. Transitions are billed per object, so the one-time fee could exceed what the colder class saves. Deleting them may be the better lever.

mcq.q: Why do S3 Intelligent-Tiering and GCS Autoclass skip objects under 128 KB?
options: Per-object fees can exceed per-byte savings for tiny objects
Small objects are always hot and read too often
Colder classes cannot store objects under 128 KB
Small objects are already compressed by the service
mcq.why: Transition and monitoring fees are charged per object while savings scale with bytes, so for tiny objects the fees win.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
hook: An optimization saves $10,000 a month. Should you do it? Not until you know one more number.
title: Payback period: under 3 months yes, over 12 be wary
body: Every storage optimization has a one-time cost: transitions, data rewrites, engineering time. Divide it by the monthly saving and you get the **payback period**. Under 3 months is an easy yes. Over 12 months needs a strong reason, because your access pattern may change before it pays back. Tiering a large photo store can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars upfront and still pay back in under a month.
takeaway: A saving you won't collect before the world changes is not a saving.
deeper:
**It makes projects comparable:** A migration that saves $600,000 a month and costs $300,000 once pays back in two weeks. One that saves $10,000 a month but needs a year of engineering and a costly rewrite may never pay back.

**Why 12 months is the warning line:** Storage decisions rest on assumptions about access patterns, object sizes and growth. A new feature that reads old data, or a price change, can break them. The longer the payback, the more time for a saving to turn into a loss.

**Count everything:** Per-object transition fees, compute to recompress or re-encode, temporary double storage during migration, engineering time. Leaving out engineering time is an easy way to make a mediocre optimization look good.

**Use it:** Sort candidate projects by payback period and start with the fastest.

quiz.q: Project A saves $50,000 a month and costs $1 million once. Project B saves $20,000 a month and costs $30,000. Which first, and what is each payback?
quiz.a: B first: it pays back in 1.5 months, an easy yes. A takes 20 months, past the 12-month line, so it needs a strong reason, since access patterns may change before then.

mcq.q: Why should a storage optimization with a payback over 12 months face extra scrutiny?
options: Access patterns may change before it pays back
Cloud providers reprice storage classes every year
Drives must be replaced within 12 months
Lifecycle rules expire after a year and must be redone
mcq.why: Long paybacks rest on assumptions about access, object size and growth that can shift, leaving the one-time cost unrecovered.

hook: There are a dozen ways to cut a storage bill. Every one does one of just two things. Which two?
title: Cut storage cost two ways: fewer bytes or cheaper bytes
body: Storage cost is bytes times price per byte, so there are only two ways to cut it. **Fewer bytes**: delete unused data and set TTLs, compress, deduplicate, keep fewer replicas, use erasure coding. **Cheaper bytes**: tier to colder classes, buy denser drives and SMR, pick the right media, flash or disk. Some levers do both. Knowing which branch a lever sits on tells you what it can and cannot fix.
takeaway: Make bytes disappear first, then make the survivors cheap.
deeper:
**A checklist for any review:** For each dataset, ask three questions. Can some bytes disappear? Can the rest get smaller? Can they sit on cheaper media or a cheaper class?

**Every lever has a bill:** Erasure coding stores fewer bytes than replication but costs CPU, network and IOPS. Tiering makes bytes cheaper but adds retrieval and transition fees. Denser drives lower $/TB but also IOPS per TB. Compression shrinks bytes but costs CPU on write and read.

**Order matters:** Delete first, so you never pay to compress, deduplicate or tier bytes that shouldn't exist. Compress before tiering so every tier stores fewer bytes, though transition fees are charged per object, not per byte.

**Where to start:** Retention hygiene and compression are the cheapest levers because they need no new hardware. Structural work like erasure coding comes later.

quiz.q: A team plans to tier 2 PB of old staging data to Glacier now and compress it later. What order would you suggest instead, and why?
quiz.a: Delete what isn't needed first, then compress, then tier. Deleting avoids paying to move or shrink bytes that shouldn't exist, and staging data without a TTL is classic waste.

mcq.q: Which lever makes bytes cheaper rather than storing fewer of them?
options: Tiering to colder storage classes
Erasure coding instead of replication
Deduplication of identical chunks
Compression with zstd
mcq.why: Tiering keeps the same bytes but pays a lower price per GB. The other three reduce the number of physical bytes stored.

hook: One scheme survives 2 lost pieces at 3× storage. Another survives 4 at 1.4×. What's the trick?
title: Erasure coding: survive more losses on less disk
body: Replication buys each tolerated failure with a full copy: 3× storage survives 2 losses. **Erasure coding** splits data into k data pieces and adds m parity pieces. Any k of the k+m pieces rebuild the data, so it survives losing any m. Overhead is (k+m)/k. **RS(10,4)**, a Reed-Solomon code, stores 14 units for every 10 of data, 1.4× overhead, and survives 4 lost pieces.
takeaway: Replication pays a full copy per failure. Parity pays a fraction.
deeper:
**The table:**
3× replication (HDFS default, Haystack): 3.0×, tolerates 2.
RS(6,3) (HDFS 3 default EC policy): 1.5×, tolerates 3.
RS(10,4) (f4 within a datacenter, Meta cold storage): 1.4×, tolerates 4.
RS(9,6) (Tectonic long-lived data): about 1.67×, tolerates 6.
LRC(12,2,2) (Azure Storage): about 1.33×, any 3 plus many 4-failure patterns.

**The dials:** A larger k lowers overhead but makes each repair read more pieces. A larger m improves tolerance but raises overhead. Tectonic's RS(9,6) pays more than RS(10,4) to tolerate 6 losses for long-lived data.

**The payoff:** Moving from 3× replication to erasure coding at 1.33× to 1.67× roughly halves hardware cost, with fault tolerance as good or better.

**The catch:** Parity is not free to use. Every repair reads k pieces instead of one copy, so erasure coding shifts cost from disk to network, CPU and IOPS.

quiz.q: You need to survive 4 simultaneous disk losses. How much storage does replication need, versus RS(10,4)?
quiz.a: Replication needs 5 full copies, 5× storage, to survive 4 losses. RS(10,4) survives 4 at 1.4×, because any 10 of its 14 pieces rebuild the data.

mcq.q: What is the storage overhead of an RS(6,3) erasure code?
mcq.why: Overhead is (k+m)/k = (6+3)/6 = 1.5×. RS(6,3) is the HDFS 3 default erasure coding policy.

hook: Meta's Haystack kept three copies of every photo. Its real storage multiplier was not 3. What was it?

predict.q: Haystack kept 3 replicas of each photo, each on RAID-6 disks. What was its effective replication factor?

title: Haystack's 3 replicas really cost 3.6×
body: Meta's Haystack photo store kept 3 replicas of each photo, and every replica sat on RAID-6 disks, which add their own parity at about 1.2×. Redundancy stacks by multiplying, so the **effective replication factor**, physical bytes per logical byte, was 3 × 1.2 = 3.6. Meta's f4 then brought warm data down to 2.8, using RS(10,4) at 1.4× stored in two datacenters. Later it reached 2.1.
takeaway: Redundancy multiplies across layers. Count every layer, or you undercount the bill.
deeper:
**The honest metric:** A system can advertise three copies while each copy hides parity underneath in RAID. Effective replication factor multiplies the layers together, so it shows the true cost.

**Why f4 existed:** Haystack was built for hot photos that need fast reads, where full replicas make sense. But photos cool quickly after upload, and keeping every old photo at 3.6× wasted capacity. f4 was built as a warm BLOB store for that cooler data.

**The step to 2.8:** Inside each datacenter, RS(10,4) replaced replicas: 1.4× overhead, tolerating 4 lost pieces, covering disk, host and rack failures. A second full copy in another datacenter covered the loss of a whole datacenter: 1.4 × 2 = 2.8.

**What came next:** f4 then replaced that second copy with something cheaper and reached 2.1 without giving up datacenter-level protection.

quiz.q: A vendor pitches "two replicas" for your archive. Each replica lives on a RAID-6 array with 1.2× parity. What is the effective replication factor, and why ask?
quiz.a: 2 × 1.2 = 2.4. Redundancy stacks multiplicatively across layers, so the advertised copy count understates the physical bytes you pay for.

mcq.q: Why was Haystack's effective replication factor 3.6 rather than 3?
options: Each replica sat on RAID-6 disks with about 1.2× parity
A fourth replica was kept in a backup datacenter
Photos were stored in several resized versions
Deleted photos stayed on disk until compaction ran
mcq.why: Stacked redundancy multiplies: 3 replicas × 1.2 RAID-6 overhead = 3.6 physical bytes per logical byte.

hook: Meta wanted photos to survive losing a whole datacenter without paying for two full copies. How?
title: f4's XOR trick: datacenter-proof at 2.1×

stat.label: storage f4 saved in 2014 (65+ PB logical data)

body: Two full erasure-coded copies in two datacenters cost 2.8×. **f4** found a cheaper way. It puts two different volumes, each at 1.4×, in two datacenters. A third datacenter stores the **XOR** of the two, also at 1.4×. Three blocks of 1.4 protect two volumes: (1.4 × 2 + 1.4) / 2 = 2.1. Lose any one datacenter and its volume is rebuilt from the other two.
takeaway: Give each layer of redundancy one failure to cover, and never pay twice.
deeper:
**How XOR recovers data:** Combine volume A and volume B bit by bit and you get A XOR B. If A is lost, B XOR (A XOR B) gives back A. The same works for B. One XOR volume replaces a full second copy for each of two volumes, turning 2.8× into 2.1×.

**Each layer has one job:** RS(10,4) inside each datacenter handles disk, host and rack failures locally, with no cross-datacenter traffic. The XOR layer handles the rare loss of a whole datacenter. No capacity is spent twice on the same failure.

**The catch:** Recovery after a datacenter loss is expensive. Rebuilding means reading from two other datacenters across the wide-area network. For warm data that is rarely read, that trade is worth the capacity it saves.

quiz.q: Datacenter 1, holding volume A, burns down. Datacenter 2 holds volume B; datacenter 3 holds A XOR B. Walk through the recovery and its main cost.
quiz.a: Read B from datacenter 2 and A XOR B from datacenter 3, then XOR them to get A. The cost is heavy cross-datacenter reads over the wide-area network during the rebuild.

mcq.q: How does f4 reach 2.1× while still surviving the loss of a whole datacenter?
options: A third datacenter stores the XOR of two volumes
Each datacenter keeps half of every volume
It stores two copies at 1.05× each in two datacenters
It relies on RAID-6 inside every datacenter
mcq.why: The XOR plus the surviving volume rebuilds the lost one, so three 1.4× blocks protect two volumes: (1.4 × 2 + 1.4) / 2 = 2.1.

hook: Repairing one lost fragment in a Reed-Solomon code means reading many others. How did Azure cut that?
title: Azure's LRC: 1.33× overhead and cheaper repairs
body: In an RS(k,m) code, rebuilding one lost fragment means reading k others, which costs disk and network. Azure Storage's **Local Reconstruction Codes (LRC)**, Best Paper at USENIX ATC 2012, reach about 1.33× overhead with an LRC(12,2,2) layout and reduce how many fragments a rebuild must read. In open source, HDFS 3's default erasure coding policy, RS(6,3), cuts storage overhead from 200% to about 50%.
takeaway: Overhead is paid once. Repair reads are paid on every failure.
deeper:
**How LRC shortens repair:** It adds local parities computed over smaller groups of fragments. A common single-fragment failure is rebuilt from its small local group instead of k fragments across the whole stripe. LRC(12,2,2) tolerates any 3 failures plus many 4-failure patterns.

**Two ways to say overhead:** HDFS counts extra bytes. 3× replication stores 200% extra beyond the data; RS(6,3) stores 50% extra, 3 parity pieces for 6 data pieces. Same idea as 3.0× versus 1.5×.

**Not exotic:** Erasure coding is standard in major cloud storage and in open-source HDFS. The engineering is in paying its other bills: CPU, network on repairs, extra IOPS on writes, and missing features.

**The catch:** Low overhead alone doesn't make a code cheap to run. Repair traffic recurs on every failure, for the life of the data.

quiz.q: Two codes have similar overhead. Code X rebuilds a lost fragment by reading 12 others; code Y reads 6. Your cluster loses disks daily. Which do you pick, and why?
quiz.a: Code Y. Repairs happen constantly, so fewer fragments read per rebuild means less disk and network traffic. That is the advantage Azure's LRC adds over plain Reed-Solomon.

mcq.q: What problem does Azure's LRC solve beyond lowering storage overhead?
options: It reduces how many fragments a rebuild must read
It removes the CPU cost of encoding writes
It lets erasure-coded files support append
It avoids storing any parity for cold data
mcq.why: Local parities let a lost fragment be rebuilt from a small group rather than k fragments, cutting repair reads and network traffic.

hook: Erasure coding can cut storage by half or more. So why doesn't everything use it?
title: Erasure coding pays in CPU, network, IOPS and features
body: Erasure coding saves capacity but charges in other currencies. **CPU**: encode on write, decode on repair. **Network**: reading a damaged or missing piece means fetching k others, and HDFS notes most EC operations go off-rack. **IOPS**: one logical write touches k+m disks. Features: HDFS EC files do not support append or hflush. To dodge the IOPS cost, Meta's Tectonic writes small appends as replicas and re-encodes to RS(10,4) after the block is sealed.
takeaway: Replicate while data is hot and changing. Encode it once it's sealed.
deeper:
**Why Tectonic waits:** Encoding small writes directly would need 14 IOs instead of 3: one per piece of RS(10,4) versus one per replica. Replicating first and encoding sealed blocks avoids that penalty.

**The repair tax:** With replication, a lost copy is restored by reading one other copy. With RS(10,4), you read 10 pieces, usually from other racks. That is why the playbook lists rebuild network and CPU as this lever's risk and rates its effort high: it is serious platform work.

**The design rule:** Use replication for hot, small, changing data and erasure coding for large, sealed, cooler data. Many systems do both over an object's life: replicated while it is written and read heavily, encoded once it is sealed and cooling.

**The catch:** On HDFS, choosing EC also means giving up append and hflush.

quiz.q: A team wants to erasure-code an HDFS directory where a service appends log lines all day. What two problems will they hit?
quiz.a: HDFS EC files don't support append or hflush, so the appender breaks. And every small write would touch k+m disks, multiplying IOPS. This data should stay replicated until sealed.

mcq.q: Why does Tectonic replicate small appends first and erasure-code only after a block is sealed?
options: Encoding small writes directly needs 14 IOs instead of 3
Replicas compress better than erasure-coded pieces
Sealed blocks can move to cheaper SMR drives
Erasure coding needs a fixed 1 GB block size
mcq.why: Under RS(10,4) each small write touches all 14 pieces; with 3 replicas it touches 3. Encoding sealed blocks avoids that IOPS penalty.

section: 12.4.2 The IOPS-per-TB trap: when bigger drives cost more
hook: Hard drives keep getting bigger. For some workloads, that makes storage more expensive. How?
title: Bigger drives, same IOPS: 6× fewer IOPS per TB

stat.label: fewer IOPS per TB: 24 TB drive vs 4 TB drive

body: A hard drive's random IOPS stays roughly flat, about 80 to 200, because a mechanical arm has to move. Capacity keeps growing. So **IOPS per TB** falls. Meta's f4 used 4 TB drives with about 80 usable IOPS: 20 IOPS per TB. A 24 TB drive with the same 80 IOPS gives about 3.3. If your data needs more IOPS per TB than that, you buy extra drives for IOPS and leave their space empty.
takeaway: When you buy drives for IOPS, you pay for arms, not platters.
deeper:
**When it bites:** Every TB of hot data generates some reads per second. If drives supply fewer IOPS per TB than the data demands, they run out of performance before they run out of space.

**The trap:** Now the drive's price per TB stops mattering, because you are buying it for its IOPS. A 24 TB drive that is only 20% full costs five times its sticker price per stored byte.

**Who wins, who loses:** For cold data that is rarely read, bigger drives are pure savings. For hot, random-access data, they can raise the effective cost.

**The catch:** Drive purchases are usually planned by capacity alone. The trap stays invisible until the cluster hits its IOPS ceiling with disks still mostly empty.

quiz.q: Your hot store needs 20 IOPS per TB. Procurement swaps 4 TB drives for 24 TB drives at the same 80 IOPS each. What happens?
quiz.a: Each 80-IOPS drive can serve only 4 TB at 20 IOPS per TB, so every 24 TB drive ends up about one-sixth full. You pay for capacity you can't use.

mcq.q: Why does IOPS per TB fall as hard drives grow?
options: Random IOPS per drive stays roughly flat while capacity rises
Larger drives spin more slowly to save power
Bigger platters need more error correction per read
Controllers cap IOPS at a fixed number per TB
mcq.why: A drive's random IOPS is set by its mechanics, roughly 80 to 200, so spreading more TB over the same IOPS lowers IOPS per TB.

section: 12.4.2 The IOPS-per-TB trap: when bigger drives cost more
hook: Haystack never changed its replication scheme, yet its effective replication rose from 3.6× to 5.3×. How?

predict.q: Haystack's replication scheme never changed, yet its effective replication factor rose from 3.6× to 5.3×. Why?
options: Drives bought for IOPS sat partly empty
A fourth replica was added for safety
RAID-6 parity grew with bigger drives

title: How Haystack drifted from 3.6× to 5.3× unchanged
body: Meta's Tectonic paper shows the IOPS-per-TB trap in production. As drives grew, IOPS per TB fell, and Haystack, the hot photo store, became **IOPS-bound**: its drives ran out of random reads before they filled. Meta had to add drives just for IOPS, leaving capacity unused. That empty space pushed Haystack's effective replication factor from 3.6 to 5.3, with the same 3 replicas on RAID-6 the whole time.
takeaway: Empty disk bought for speed is still disk you paid for.
deeper:
**What the metric measures:** Effective replication factor is physical capacity bought per logical byte, not the number of copies. Space bought for performance counts. Haystack still stored 3 replicas on RAID-6, but with disks partly empty, each logical byte used 5.3 bytes of capacity.

**The chain:**
1. Drives grew bigger; IOPS per drive stayed flat.
2. IOPS per TB fell.
3. Haystack needed extra drives just for IOPS.
4. The unused capacity raised physical bytes per logical byte.

**The architecture lesson:** Separate hot and cold data. Hot data belongs on media sized for IOPS, possibly flash; cold data belongs on the densest drives. Mix them on one tier and you get a compromise that is wrong for both, and it worsens with every larger drive.

quiz.q: Your team keeps a hot store on HDD and upgrades to double-size drives every few years. Nobody touches the replication config. Why might cost per logical byte still rise?
quiz.a: IOPS per TB halves with each upgrade. If the store is IOPS-bound, you must add drives for IOPS that sit partly empty, raising physical bytes per logical byte, as happened to Haystack.

mcq.q: What does Haystack's rise from 3.6× to 5.3× show about effective replication factor?
options: It counts capacity bought for IOPS, not just copies
It rises whenever drives are swapped for newer models
It is set only by the replication and RAID scheme
It measures replicas across datacenters, not disks
mcq.why: Extra drives bought for IOPS sat partly empty. That unused capacity counts as physical bytes per logical byte.

section: 12.4.2 The IOPS-per-TB trap: when bigger drives cost more
hook: A drive that fits 10-20% more data at similar cost sounds like free money. What's the catch?
title: SMR packs 10-20% more per drive if you write in order
body: **SMR** (shingled magnetic recording) overlaps tracks like roof shingles to fit more data. The catch: writes must be sequential within fixed zones. Dropbox was one of the first large companies to run SMR in production, from September 2018. SMR gave roughly 10% to 20% more data per drive at similar cost, and the new storage design saved more than 20% overall versus the previous generation. Dropbox staged the slow writes on an SSD cache.
takeaway: Dense media rewards workloads that never edit in place.
deeper:
**Why shingles:** Each new track partly covers the one before it, like shingles on a roof. Rewriting one track in place would damage its overlapping neighbor, so writes must go in order through a zone. The mapping is exact: you can add a row at the end, not swap one out in the middle.

**Why it fit Dropbox:** Its storage is mostly large, immutable blobs written sequentially. The SSD cache absorbs incoming writes, which then go to SMR in order.

**Where it fails:** SMR sharpens the IOPS-per-TB trade. More capacity behind the same arm means even fewer IOPS per TB, and random writes are especially bad.

**The catch:** The 20% saving was not SMR alone. The same design went from 60 to 100 disks per machine with the same CPU and memory.

quiz.q: A team wants SMR drives under a database that updates small rows in place all day. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: SMR requires sequential writes within zones because tracks overlap. Random in-place updates clash with that and collapse write performance, on top of already lower IOPS per TB.

mcq.q: Why did SMR suit Dropbox's storage?
options: Mostly large, immutable blobs written sequentially
Mostly small records updated in place
Mostly hot data read at random
Mostly metadata that needs low latency
mcq.why: SMR writes must be sequential within zones. Dropbox's large immutable blobs, staged through an SSD cache, match that constraint.

section: 12.4.2 The IOPS-per-TB trap: when bigger drives cost more
hook: Flash costs several times more per TB than disk. For some stores it is still the cheaper choice. When?
title: Buy storage by the cheaper of $/TB and $/IOPS
body: Price per TB is the wrong unit for a storage decision. The right one is the cheaper of **$/TB** and **$/IOPS** for your workload. Cold archives are capacity-bound, so buy the biggest, densest drives. Hot small-object stores are IOPS-bound, so big drives waste money, and flash may be cheaper overall despite costing several times more per TB. Whichever constraint binds first sets how many devices you buy.
takeaway: The constraint that binds first decides which price you're really paying.
deeper:
**How to apply it:** Estimate two needs: how many TB the data takes and how many IOPS its access pattern demands. Work out how many devices of each type satisfy both. The device count follows whichever constraint binds first, and cost follows the count.

**Cold archive:** Capacity binds. A few IOPS per TB is plenty, so the densest HDD means the fewest devices.

**Hot small objects:** User profiles or message indexes are IOPS-bound. You might need many mostly-empty HDDs where a few SSDs would supply the IOPS with capacity to spare. At that point flash wins on total cost.

**The cautionary tale:** Haystack drifting to 5.3× is what happens when a hot workload is bought as if capacity were the only constraint.

quiz.q: A store holds 10 TB but needs 50,000 random IOPS. HDDs give about 100 IOPS each. Why might flash beat HDD on total cost?
quiz.a: You'd need about 500 HDDs just for the IOPS, almost all empty. A few SSDs meet the IOPS with capacity to spare, so despite a higher $/TB they cost less overall.

mcq.q: Which unit should drive a storage media decision?
options: The cheaper of $/TB and $/IOPS for the workload
The lowest $/TB available on the market
The lowest $/IOPS regardless of capacity
The highest capacity per drive slot
mcq.why: Device count is set by whichever of capacity or IOPS binds first, so the price that matters depends on the workload.

hook: Most real storage systems are neither all-flash nor all-disk. What decides which byte goes where?
title: Route data to flash or disk by what limits it
body: Flash costs more per TB than disk but gives orders of magnitude more IOPS per TB. So route data by its limit. **Capacity-bound** data, like photos older than a month, lake files and backups, goes on HDD or colder. **IOPS-bound** data, like profiles, message indexes, metadata and hot small objects, goes on flash. Mixed workloads use HDD for the bulk plus a flash cache or flash tier for the hot part.
takeaway: Put the few busy bytes on flash so the quiet ones live on disk.
deeper:
**Real systems mix:** Meta's Tectonic storage nodes each carry a 1 TB SSD for metadata and caching hot chunks, with bulk data on hard drives. Google's Colossus places hot data on flash and moves it to disk as it ages.

**Why mixing works:** A small fraction of data gets most of the accesses. Put that fraction on flash and the HDD tier can be sized purely for capacity with the densest drives. You avoid all-flash overpaying for capacity and all-HDD overprovisioning for IOPS, as happened to Haystack.

**Metadata first:** It is small, read on almost every operation and randomly accessed, the classic IOPS-bound data. Slow metadata slows every request, so it goes on flash even in disk-based systems.

**Where it sits:** In the lever tree, right media is a cheaper-bytes lever.

quiz.q: You're designing a photo service: profile records, photo metadata, and 40 PB of photos where most views hit the last month's uploads. What goes on flash and what on disk?
quiz.a: Flash: profiles, metadata and recent hot photos, which are IOPS-bound. Disk: the bulk of older photos, which are capacity-bound. A flash cache or tier in front of HDD covers the mix.

mcq.q: Which data is IOPS-bound and belongs on flash?
options: Message indexes and metadata
Photos older than a month
Data lake files
Backups of similar machines
mcq.why: Indexes and metadata are small and randomly read on nearly every request, so IOPS, not capacity, limits them.

hook: One of the cheapest storage cost levers needs no new drives, no new servers and no datacenter space. Which?
title: Compression: a cost lever that needs no hardware
body: Most levers need hardware or platform work. **Compression** needs software. **zstd** (Zstandard), open-sourced by Facebook in 2016, compresses 3 to 5 times faster than zlib at the same ratio, or 10% to 15% smaller at the same speed. Its current benchmark shows level 1 at a 2.896 ratio versus zlib level 1 at 2.743, with about 4 times faster decompression. Faster codecs make compression affordable in more places.
takeaway: Spend CPU once on cold data. Spend it lightly on hot data.
deeper:
**Why it pays fast:** No drives, servers or space to buy, so it ships as a software change with a short payback. The playbook rates it low effort, with CPU as the main risk, and logs and lake tables as the best first targets.

**Choosing a level:** The cost is CPU on write and read. For cold data, use a higher level: spend CPU once, save bytes for years. For hot data, use a fast level, because CPU cost recurs on every access.

**Why speed matters:** With decompression about 4 times faster than zlib, you can compress hot data that used to be too expensive to decompress on every read.

**The catch:** 2.896 versus 2.743 looks modest. Across petabytes, a few percent smaller output plus much lower CPU is real money.

quiz.q: You keep 5 PB of logs for 7 years and a 50 TB hot cache read thousands of times a second. Which compression level suits each?
quiz.a: Logs: a high level, since CPU is spent once and the bytes are saved for years. Hot cache: a fast level, since decompression cost recurs on every read.

mcq.q: What does zstd offer over zlib, per Facebook's 2016 announcement?
options: 3 to 5 times faster at the same ratio
Twice the ratio at the same speed
No CPU cost on decompression
Better ratios only on encrypted data
mcq.why: zstd compresses 3 to 5 times faster than zlib at the same ratio, or 10% to 15% smaller at the same speed.

hook: Compress a single 1 KB JSON record and you barely save anything. What changes the answer?

predict.q: Facebook's ~1 KB JSON records compressed at 2.8×. With a trained dictionary, the ratio became about:

title: A trained dictionary took 1 KB records from 2.8× to 6.9×

stat.label: ratio on ~1 KB JSON with a trained dictionary

body: Small records compress poorly: a compressor has little data in which to find repeats. **Dictionary compression** fixes that. Train a dictionary on sample records, capturing common strings like field names, and give it to both compressor and decompressor. In Facebook's example, roughly 1 KB JSON records went from a 2.8× ratio to 6.9×. That matters for a profile store, where every record is small and shaped alike.
takeaway: Teach the compressor your schema once instead of storing it in every record.
deeper:
**Why it works:** A general compressor learns patterns as it goes, so on a 1 KB record it finishes before learning much. The dictionary supplies that knowledge upfront. Records that share a schema, like JSON with the same keys, benefit most: the repeated field names live in the dictionary, not in every record.

**The size of the win:** 2.8× to 6.9× means storing well under half the bytes for the same data. Across a billion small profiles, that is a large saving with no hardware change.

**The operational cost:** The dictionary must be stored and versioned, because every record compressed with it needs it to decompress. If record structure drifts, retrain, and keep old dictionaries for old records.

**Where it comes from:** zstd supports trained dictionaries natively; the 1 KB JSON example is from Facebook's 2016 announcement of the library.

quiz.q: You enable dictionary compression on a profile store, retrain a new dictionary, then delete the old one. What breaks?
quiz.a: Every record compressed with the old dictionary can no longer be decompressed. Dictionaries must be versioned and kept as long as any record depends on them.

mcq.q: Why does a trained dictionary help 1 KB records far more than large files?
options: Small records give the compressor too little data to learn repeats
Large files cannot use dictionaries in zstd
Dictionaries only work on data under 1 KB
Small records are always less random than large ones
mcq.why: A dictionary supplies common strings such as field names upfront, which a compressor can't learn from 1 KB alone.

hook: Same data, same values. Stored one way it's huge; stored another way it's a fraction. What changed?
title: Store data by column and it compresses far better
body: Row formats interleave unrelated values: a name, a timestamp, a country code, then the next record. **Columnar formats** such as Parquet, ORC and Google's Capacitor store each column's values together. Values in one column are similar, so they compress far better. Encodings like dictionary and **run-length** multiply the effect, and Capacitor goes further by reordering rows to group similar values.
takeaway: Layout decides compressibility before the compressor ever runs.
deeper:
**Dictionary encoding:** Repeated values become small integer codes, so a column with a few hundred distinct values costs a few bits per row.

**Run-length encoding:** A repeated value is stored once with a count. It shines when identical values sit next to each other.

**Row reordering:** Capacitor sorts or clusters rows so more identical values become adjacent, which makes run-length encoding stronger still. A general compressor like zstd can then run on the encoded columns, compounding the saving.

**The payoff:** The playbook lists compression at 10% to 15% over zlib with zstd, and more with columnar formats, at low effort with CPU as the risk. Lake tables are a best first target. The same data as JSON rows and as sorted columns can differ enormously in size without changing a single value.

quiz.q: A lake table stores events as JSON rows, and its country column has 200 distinct values. Which two changes would shrink it most?
quiz.a: Convert to a columnar format like Parquet so the column is dictionary-encoded into small codes, and sort rows by country so run-length encoding collapses the repeats.

mcq.q: Why does Capacitor reorder rows?
options: To put identical values next to each other for run-length encoding
To speed up writes by appending in arrival order
To spread hot rows across more disks
To make each row readable without its schema
mcq.why: Run-length encoding stores a repeated value once with a count, so clustering identical values makes it far more effective.

hook: A million users upload the same viral video. How many copies does a smart store keep, and how does it know?
title: Deduplication: name data by its hash, store it once
body: **Deduplication** stores identical content once. **Content-addressed** systems name each chunk by a hash of its content, so two identical uploads get the same name and map to one stored chunk. The second upload adds a reference, not new bytes. It works best when many users store the same files: shared attachments, forwarded videos, backups of similar machines. The saving depends entirely on how much duplication exists.
takeaway: When the name comes from the content, a duplicate finds itself.
deeper:
**Detection is cheap:** Hash incoming data and look it up. If the name already exists, so does the content. No full-file comparison is needed.

**Where it pays:** A messaging app where one video is forwarded millions of times can store it once. Backups of machines running the same operating system repeat most of their bytes. A set of unique user photos has little to deduplicate.

**The playbook view:** Medium effort, savings that depend on the duplicate rate, and a blunt risk: garbage collection bugs lose data. Best first targets are backups and shared attachments.

**The catch:** Dedup is not free to run. Hashing, reference tracking and safer deletion cost engineering, so reserve it for data where measurements show a real duplicate rate.

quiz.q: Your storage team proposes dedup for a bucket of original, unique user photos. What should you ask before approving?
quiz.a: What is the measured duplicate rate? Unique photos have little to deduplicate, so you'd pay hashing and reference-tracking complexity, plus deletion risk, for little saving.

mcq.q: How does content addressing detect duplicates?
options: Identical content hashes to the same chunk name
A nightly job compares every file byte by byte
Users tag files they know are duplicates
Files with the same name and size are merged
mcq.why: Each chunk is named by a hash of its content, so a duplicate upload maps to the existing chunk and adds only a reference.

hook: Deduplication saves space. It also turns a routine delete into a way to lose someone else's data. How?
title: Dedup's catch: encrypted data and risky deletes
body: Dedup works poorly on already-compressed or encrypted data, where identical content rarely produces identical bytes, so hashes don't match. It also changes deletion. You can't delete a chunk until nobody references it, so you need **reference counting** or garbage collection. A bug in that bookkeeping can delete a chunk someone still needs. Dedup trades storage savings for correctness risk in every delete.
takeaway: Leaked references waste space. Lost references destroy data.
deeper:
**Why encrypted data resists:** Encryption is designed to make output look random, and different keys produce different bytes for the same input. Compression can shift byte boundaries so small differences change everything after them. Dedup works best on data before it is encrypted or compressed.

**Why deletion gets hard:** Without dedup, deleting a file frees its bytes. With dedup, deleting one user's file only decrements a reference; the chunk lives until the last reference goes. Counts can drift after crashes or races, and a collector scanning for unreferenced chunks can race with an upload that just started referencing an old one.

**The asymmetry:** A bug that over-counts wastes space. A bug that under-counts deletes data users believe is safe. That is why the playbook lists GC bugs losing data as dedup's risk.

quiz.q: A dedup store's garbage collector deletes chunk X at the same moment a new upload of identical content is mapped to X. What happens, and which kind of bug is it?
quiz.a: The new upload now points at a deleted chunk, so its data is lost. It's an under-counted reference, the dangerous direction: it destroys data instead of merely wasting space.

mcq.q: Why does deduplication work poorly on encrypted data?
options: Identical content rarely produces identical encrypted bytes
Encrypted chunks are too large to hash efficiently
Encryption keys must be deduplicated separately
Encrypted data cannot be split into chunks
mcq.why: Encryption makes output look random, so the same content under different keys gives different bytes and different hashes.

section: 12.4.6 Retention hygiene: delete what you do not need
hook: The cheapest storage lever doesn't compress, move or re-encode a single byte. What is it?
title: The cheapest byte is the one you delete
body: At most companies, a large share of stored bytes is waste. Old table snapshots nobody will roll back to. Orphan files left by failed jobs. Staging and temp data with no **TTL** (time to live, an automatic expiry). One-off dataset copies made for an analysis years ago. Old object versions in buckets with versioning on and no lifecycle rule for non-current versions. **Retention hygiene** means finding and deleting them.
takeaway: Delete a byte and you delete its replicas, backups, fees and power too.
deeper:
**How each pile grows:** Table formats that keep snapshots for time travel pile up versions unless snapshots expire. Failed jobs leave partial output no table references, so nothing reads or deletes it. Temp data without a TTL outlives the job that made it. Analyst copies outlive the analysis. Bucket versioning keeps every overwritten or deleted object as a billed non-current version unless a rule expires it.

**Why deletion beats every lever:** It removes the bytes and all their multipliers: replicas, backups, tiering fees and energy. Retention hygiene and compression are the cheapest levers because neither needs new hardware.

**The catch:** The risk is deleting data someone needed. Start with the safest targets: temp and staging data and old snapshots. The playbook rates the saving high but variable, at low to medium effort.

quiz.q: A versioned bucket is overwritten nightly by a job. Its live data stays at 10 TB, yet billed storage keeps climbing. Why?
quiz.a: Each overwrite keeps the old object as a non-current version, billed like normal data. With no lifecycle rule to expire non-current versions, they pile up forever.

mcq.q: Which is the safest first target for deleting unused data?
options: Temp and staging data and old snapshots
Production tables with no reads this week
Backups older than one month
The only replica in a second region
mcq.why: The main risk is deleting needed data, so start where there is clearly no future use: temp, staging and old snapshots.

section: 12.4.6 Retention hygiene: delete what you do not need
hook: A team runs a big cleanup, reclaims a pile of space and declares victory. A year later the waste is back. Why?
title: Retention is a platform job, not a cleanup project
body: Cleanup projects reclaim space once. Then nothing changes in how data is created, and the waste regrows. LinkedIn's **OpenHouse**, a table management platform, runs snapshot expiration, orphan file deletion and retention as platform jobs for exactly this reason. Treat retention like a feature with an owner, not a one-time cleanup. A platform that enforces retention continuously keeps waste from building up at all.
takeaway: Cleanup is an event. Retention is a feature. Only features last.
deeper:
**The cleanup cycle:** Someone notices the bill. A project gets staffed, spends weeks finding and deleting waste, declares victory and disbands. The same kinds of waste return, because the way data is created never changed.

**The platform version:** Snapshot expiration runs on a schedule for every table. Orphan file deletion finds files no table references and removes them. Retention policies are declared per dataset and enforced centrally. Teams don't have to remember anything.

**The broader principle:** A storage efficiency program succeeds when the platform makes the cheap choice the default: TTLs required at creation, lifecycle rules on by default, compaction and retention run centrally, owner names next to large datasets. OpenHouse is that idea applied to lake tables.
