**The catch:** The platform job needs an owner too, or it becomes the next thing nobody maintains.

quiz.q: Last year a cleanup deleted 30% of your lake storage. It's back to the old size. What would you change so it sticks?
quiz.a: Make retention a platform feature: scheduled snapshot expiration, orphan file deletion and per-dataset retention enforced centrally, as LinkedIn's OpenHouse does, instead of another one-off project.

mcq.q: Which jobs does LinkedIn's OpenHouse run as platform jobs?
options: Snapshot expiration, orphan file deletion and retention
Erasure coding, tiering and replication
Compression, deduplication and compaction
Chargeback, quotas and showback
mcq.why: OpenHouse runs retention work centrally so waste doesn't regrow when teams forget to clean up.

hook: A database has 3 replicas per region, a backup, a lake copy and a warm cache copy. How many does it need?
title: For every copy, ask which failure it covers
body: Copies pile up because each is added by a different team for a different reason. A common result: 3 replicas in every region, plus a backup, plus a lake copy, plus a warm cache copy. For each one, ask what failure it protects against and whether another copy already covers it. Meta's f4 is the model: it cut 3.6× to 2.1× by deciding which failures, disk, host, rack or datacenter, each **layer of redundancy** covers.
takeaway: Two copies guarding against the same failure is one copy of waste.
deeper:
**Different copies, different jobs:** Regional replicas guard against zone and region failures. Backups guard against logical corruption and accidental deletion, which replicas faithfully copy. A lake copy serves analytics. A cache copy serves latency. Some needs are distinct; others overlap, like two disaster-recovery copies in different systems covering the same regional failure.

**The disciplined version:** In f4, erasure coding inside a datacenter covers disk, host and rack. The cross-datacenter XOR covers datacenter loss. No layer duplicates another's job.

**The playbook view:** Low effort, one copy's cost saved per extra replica removed. The risk is lower durability if you remove the only protection against some failure. Best first targets are duplicate disaster-recovery and lake copies.

**The catch:** Replicas are not backups. Drop the backup because you have replicas, and one bad write reaches every copy.

quiz.q: An engineer says: "We have 3 replicas in each of two regions, so the nightly backup is redundant." Is it?
quiz.a: No. Replicas protect against hardware and site failures but faithfully copy corruption and accidental deletes. The backup covers those logical failures, which no replica does.

mcq.q: How did Meta's f4 reduce effective replication from 3.6× to 2.1×?
options: By assigning each redundancy layer a specific failure
By dropping datacenter-level protection for warm data
By compressing photos before storing them
By moving warm photos to tape
mcq.why: Erasure coding covered disk, host and rack; the XOR layer covered datacenter loss. No capacity paid twice for the same failure.

hook: The cloud's price includes the provider's profit margin. So why is it usually cheaper than owning?
title: Cloud usually wins until scale is huge and steady
body: A cloud storage price includes the provider's hardware, power, staff and margin. Owning skips the margin but adds a big fixed cost: a team to design, run and replace hardware. At small and medium scale, that team costs more than the margin you'd save, so the cloud is almost always cheaper once you count people. At very large, steady scale, **on-prem** can win. Real companies have gone both ways.
takeaway: Owning pays only once the margin you'd keep outgrows the team you'd need.
deeper:
**Why scale matters:** Running storage yourself is a fixed people cost. At small scale it dwarfs any hardware saving. As scale grows, hardware and power dominate, the team cost is spread thin, and the provider's margin becomes the big number you could keep.

**Why steadiness matters:** The cloud lets you pay for what you use and grow instantly. Owning means buying capacity ahead of demand. If growth is spiky or uncertain, you overbuy and waste money, or underbuy and run out.

**Three real cases:** Dropbox moved off S3 onto its own system. 37signals left S3 in 2025 despite being modest in size. Uber moved the other way, from its own Hadoop datacenters to Google Cloud.

**The catch:** Scale alone doesn't decide. Egress, team, speed and capital all tip the answer.

quiz.q: A 40-person startup storing 300 TB wants to buy its own storage arrays to "stop paying Amazon's margin". What's the flaw?
quiz.a: At that scale, the people needed to run hardware cost more than the margin saved. Under 1 PB or with unpredictable growth, the better move is staying in the cloud and optimizing tiers.

mcq.q: Why is the cloud usually cheaper at small scale despite including the provider's margin?
options: Owning needs a team whose cost outweighs the margin
Cloud providers sell storage below their own cost
Small companies get the largest volume discounts
Cloud storage needs no redundancy overhead
mcq.why: Running your own storage is a large fixed people cost. Only at large, steady scale does the margin you'd save exceed it.

hook: Dropbox moved most of its users' data off AWS onto hardware it ran itself. What did that save?
title: Dropbox's Magic Pocket saved about $74.6M in two years

stat.label: saved in 2016-17, per Dropbox's 2018 IPO filing

body: Dropbox built its own storage system, **Magic Pocket**, and by October 2015 had moved about 90% of user data onto it from AWS S3. It held over 500 PB. Dropbox's 2018 IPO filing reported that this Infrastructure Optimization saved about $39.5 million in 2016 over 2015 and a further $35.1 million in 2017. Dropbox still used AWS for a small part of its storage.
takeaway: At large, steady scale, the provider's margin is worth building a team to keep.
deeper:
**Why Dropbox fit:** Storage was its core product. Its data was very large and grew steadily and predictably. It could build and keep a storage team. And its data, mostly large immutable blobs, suited cost-optimized hardware like SMR drives and 100-disk servers.

**The hybrid result:** Dropbox did not leave the cloud entirely. Most user data moved to its own hardware, and a small part of its storage stayed on AWS.

**Why the numbers hold up:** The savings come from the company's own IPO filing, not from outside estimates.

**The catch:** Dropbox passed every test at once: scale, steadiness, a storage team, and storage as the business itself. Copy the decision without those conditions and you copy none of the savings.

quiz.q: A fintech with 2 PB of spiky data and no storage engineers cites Dropbox to justify leaving the cloud. What's missing from the comparison?
quiz.a: Dropbox's storage was its core product, very large, steady and predictable, and it could build a storage team. Spiky data and no team fail those conditions.

mcq.q: What made Dropbox a strong candidate to leave S3 for its own storage?
options: Storage was its core product at large, steady scale
AWS stopped offering the storage classes it needed
Its data was mostly small, hot records
It needed faster access to managed services
mcq.why: Dropbox had very large, predictable storage central to its business and could build a storage team, so the provider's margin was worth keeping.

hook: 37signals is no Dropbox. It still left S3 and projects millions in savings. What made it work?

predict.q: 37signals paid just under $1.5M a year for S3. Over five years on its own hardware, it projected savings of about:
options: $5 million
$1 million
$10 million

title: 37signals left S3 in 2025, projecting ~$5M saved
body: 37signals, maker of Basecamp and HEY, paid just under $1.5 million a year for S3. In 2025 it left. It bought about 18 PB of **Pure Storage** capacity across two datacenters for about $1.5 million, with support under $1 million over five years, and projected savings of nearly $5 million over five years. AWS offered a free 60-day egress window to move about 6 PB out.
takeaway: Owning can pay without huge scale: steady storage plus a willing team.
deeper:
**Why it's instructive:** 37signals is not huge. The savings came from very steady, predictable storage and a team willing to run hardware, not from exabyte scale.

**The arithmetic:** About one year's S3 bill buys the hardware. Five years of support costs under $1 million. Against roughly $7.5 million of S3 over five years, hardware plus support comes to under $2.5 million. The gap is roughly the nearly $5 million 37signals projected.

**The exit fee:** Moving petabytes out of a cloud can cost a lot in egress, which makes leaving harder. AWS's free 60-day window removed that one-time cost for about 6 PB.

**The catch:** A free window has a deadline. The migration has to fit inside it, or a delay turns into a real egress bill. Plan the data move as carefully as the hardware purchase.

quiz.q: Company Z also pays $1.5 million a year for S3, but its data doubles unpredictably every year and nobody wants to run hardware. Does the 37signals math transfer?
quiz.a: No. 37signals' savings came from very steady, predictable storage and a team willing to run hardware. Unpredictable growth and no operators remove both conditions.

mcq.q: What made 37signals' S3 exit pay off without huge scale?
options: Very steady storage and a team willing to run hardware
An exabyte-scale data platform with heavy egress
Free hardware provided by Pure Storage
A permanent waiver of AWS egress fees
mcq.why: The savings came from steady, predictable storage and willingness to operate hardware. AWS's egress waiver lasted only 60 days.

hook: More than an exabyte in each of two regions, run in-house. Then Uber chose to move it to the cloud. Why?

predict.q: Uber ran more than 1 EB per region in its own Hadoop datacenters. What did it announce in 2024?
options: Moving the platform to Google Cloud
Building a third owned region
Moving hot data to all-flash on-prem

title: Uber chose to move 1+ EB per region to Google Cloud
body: If scale alone decided, Uber would never leave its own datacenters. In 2024 it announced it would move its batch data platform, more than 1 exabyte in each of two regions, from its own Hadoop datacenters to Google Cloud, starting with **Google Cloud Storage** as the data lake. Uber valued faster access to managed services and less datacenter work. Scale alone does not decide cloud versus on-prem.
takeaway: Cost is one input. Where your engineers spend their time is another.
deeper:
**The counterexample:** Large, steady scale is where owning supposedly wins. Uber had the scale and chose the other way, because it weighed speed and focus alongside price.

**Uber versus Dropbox:** Dropbox's storage was its core product: very large, steady, predictable, with a team to run it. Uber valued managed services and less datacenter operations, and its storage cost was spread over a broader data platform rather than being the product itself.

**The three cases together:** Owning can win at large, steady scale. Dropbox saved about $74.6 million over two years; 37signals projects about $5 million over five. Uber shows large companies also move to the cloud for speed and managed services.

**The catch:** A cost model that only counts dollars per TB will get Uber's decision wrong every time.

quiz.q: Your CTO argues: "We're at exabyte scale, so on-prem is obviously cheaper, full stop." Use Uber to push back.
quiz.a: Uber had more than 1 EB per region and still chose to move to Google Cloud, valuing managed services and less datacenter work. Scale matters, but speed and focus can outweigh savings.

mcq.q: Why did Uber decide to move its batch data platform to Google Cloud despite its huge scale?
options: It valued managed services and less datacenter work
Its data was small and fast-changing
Cloud storage was cheaper than its own drives
Its Hadoop clusters could not hold an exabyte
mcq.why: Uber weighed faster access to managed services and less datacenter operations above the savings of owning; its cost was spread over a broader platform.

hook: Two companies store the same many petabytes. One should own its storage; the other shouldn't. Why?
title: Six factors tip cloud versus on-prem
body: Size is one factor of six. **Scale**: small or fast-changing favors cloud; large and steady, many PB, favors on-prem. **Growth**: spiky favors cloud; predictable favors on-prem. **Egress**: low favors cloud; high egress to users or partners favors on-prem. Team: no storage hardware team favors cloud. Speed: needing new services fast favors cloud; a stable, well-known workload favors on-prem. Capital: preferring operating expense favors cloud; spending upfront favors on-prem.
takeaway: Big and spiky rents. Big, steady and staffed can own.
deeper:
**They interact:** A company with many petabytes but spiky growth may still prefer cloud because it can't plan hardware purchases. A company with steady data but no way to hire a storage team faces operational risk that erases paper savings.

**Team means keeping one:** Hiring isn't enough. On-prem storage is a multi-year commitment, and losing expertise midway is dangerous.

**Speed and capital:** The cloud offers managed services immediately, which is what Uber valued. Capital is a finance question: on-prem means large upfront hardware purchases, while cloud spreads cost as monthly operating expense.

**Why egress tips it:** Cloud egress is billed per GB at high rates, so heavy serving to users inflates the cloud bill. That is why high egress sits on the on-prem side.

quiz.q: A company has 30 PB, predictable growth and heavy egress to partners, but prefers operating expense and can't hire hardware engineers. Which factors pull each way?
quiz.a: Toward on-prem: large steady scale, predictable growth, high egress. Toward cloud: no storage hardware team and a preference for operating expense. Without a team, the decision flow says negotiate committed-use discounts.

mcq.q: Which factor favors on-prem storage?
options: High egress to users or partners
Unpredictable, spiky growth
Needing new services quickly
Preferring operating expense
mcq.why: Cloud egress is billed per GB, so heavy serving inflates cloud bills. The other three favor staying in the cloud.

hook: Most companies should never model a cloud exit. Which ones should, and when?
title: Leave the cloud only after three gates say yes
body: Start with scale. Under 1 PB or unpredictable: stay in the cloud and optimize tiers. Many PB, steady growth and high egress: ask whether you can build and run a storage team. No: negotiate cloud **committed-use discounts**. Yes: model on-prem TCO over 5 years. If savings are still large after people and risk, consider a migration like Dropbox or 37signals. If not, negotiate discounts.
takeaway: Every no in the flow leads back to optimizing the cloud you have.
deeper:
**Deliberately conservative:** Migration is reached only after three gates: scale and stability, team capability, and a full TCO model where savings survive people and risk. Every no leads back to optimizing inside the cloud, through tiering or committed-use discounts, where you commit to a spending level in exchange for lower prices.

**Why 5 years:** It matches typical hardware life, like the 5-year drive life in the usable-TB math, so the model covers a full hardware cycle.

**What risk means:** Moving petabytes takes time, engineering and egress fees, and something can go wrong. 37signals softened one part of this with AWS's free 60-day egress window.

**The catch:** Negotiating is itself a lever. A credible on-prem TCO model strengthens your hand in discount talks even if you never migrate.

quiz.q: A company has 20 PB, steady growth, high egress and a strong storage team. Its 5-year on-prem model shows modest savings once people and migration risk are counted. What does the flow say?
quiz.a: Don't migrate. Savings that aren't large after people and risk lead to negotiating cloud committed-use discounts, and the TCO model strengthens that negotiation.

mcq.q: In the decision flow, what should a large, steady company do if it cannot build and run a storage team?
options: Negotiate cloud committed-use discounts
Migrate anyway and hire the team later
Model a 5-year on-prem TCO
Move all data to the coldest tier
mcq.why: On-prem savings depend on a capable team. Without one, the flow sends you to negotiate discounts inside the cloud.

hook: An on-prem pitch compares S3's list price with the price of hard drives. Why does it look so good?
title: Don't compare cloud list price with drive price
body: The mistake: comparing the cloud's list price with the cost of drives. Both sides are wrong. Big customers rarely pay list, and drives are a minority of TCO. The fair comparison is the cloud price **after negotiated discounts** against **full on-prem TCO**: hardware, spares, power, space, network, people, and the risk and time of the migration. The naive version flatters on-prem enormously.
takeaway: Compare what you'd really pay with everything you'd really own.
deeper:
**The cloud side:** Negotiated and committed-use discounts can cut the price well below list. A worked bill for a photo app already assumes a blended $0.05 per GB for egress against a $0.09 list price.

**The on-prem side:** Drives are one line of six. Servers, redundancy, fill headroom, spare hardware, power and cooling, space, network and staff multiply the drive cost several times.

**The migration:** Engineering months, running both systems in parallel, egress fees to move data out, and the risk of loss or downtime during the move.

**The catch:** This comparison fails every question you should ask of a cost per TB: raw or usable, which redundancy, what fill level, and whether power, space and people are included. It can overstate on-prem savings by a wide margin.

quiz.q: A slide says: "S3 is $0.023 per GB-month; drives are $0.014 per GB. On-prem saves 40%." Name three things wrong with it.
quiz.a: It uses S3 list price, not the discounted price. It compares raw drives, ignoring redundancy, fill headroom, servers, power, space, network and people. It ignores migration cost and risk.

mcq.q: What is the fair way to compare cloud and on-prem storage cost?
options: Discounted cloud price vs full on-prem TCO including migration
Cloud list price vs the cost of drives per TB
Cloud list price vs on-prem hardware and power
Discounted cloud price vs raw drive cost plus spares
mcq.why: Big customers pay discounted rates, and on-prem cost includes hardware, spares, power, space, network, people, and the risk and time of migrating.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
hook: Finance sees the storage bill every month. The engineers who created it never do. What fixes that?
title: FinOps makes engineers own their cloud cost
body: Engineers make the decisions that drive storage cost: formats, retention, replication, access patterns. If they never see the cost, they can't weigh it. **FinOps** (financial operations) makes engineering teams responsible for their cloud cost. The FinOps Foundation describes three repeating phases: Inform (see the cost), Optimize (reduce it) and Operate (make it continuous). For storage, the practices are tagging, showback and chargeback, analytics tools, quotas and unit cost metrics.
takeaway: Cost nobody sees is cost nobody manages.
deeper:
**Why it loops:** Inform makes cost visible: who owns which data, what it costs, how it's used. Optimize applies the levers: tiering, deletion, compression, right-sized replicas. Operate makes fixes stick with policies, defaults, budgets and monitoring. Data and usage keep changing, so the loop never ends.

**The storage flow:**
1. Tag every bucket and table with an owner.
2. Collect usage and access metadata.
3. Build showback dashboards per team.
4. Find waste: no-access data, orphan files, missing TTLs.
5. Apply fixes: tiering, deletion, compression.
6. Keep it fixed with chargeback and quotas.

**The idea underneath:** Accountability. FinOps puts cost next to latency and reliability as something engineers measure and manage. Engineers who choose formats, retention and replication should see what those choices cost.

quiz.q: A company ran one big optimization sprint, cut storage 40%, then moved on. Which FinOps phase did it skip, and what will happen?
quiz.a: Operate. Without continuous policies, defaults, budgets and monitoring, data and usage keep changing and the savings erode as waste regrows.

mcq.q: What are the FinOps Foundation's three phases?
options: Inform, Optimize, Operate
Tag, Charge, Enforce
Measure, Migrate, Monitor
Plan, Build, Review
mcq.why: Inform makes cost visible, Optimize reduces it, and Operate keeps it continuous. The three phases repeat.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
hook: A 2 PB bucket sits on the bill. Nobody knows whose it is, so nobody dares delete it. What was missing?
title: No tag, no owner: tagging is FinOps step one
body: **Tagging** means every bucket, volume and table carries tags naming its owner team, service and environment. Without tags, no one owns the cost. A big untagged bucket can't be charged to anyone, questioned, or safely deleted. Showback, chargeback, quotas and waste hunting all depend on knowing whose data is whose, which is why tagging is the first step of storage FinOps.
takeaway: Every byte needs a name next to it, or it lives forever.
deeper:
**How orphans happen:** A dataset created years ago by someone who has since changed teams stays on the bill indefinitely, because nobody knows whether it's safe to delete. With tags, the question has an answer, and that owner decides.

**Why the environment tag:** Non-production data often has different retention needs. Staging and test data should usually expire; production may need long retention. Tags let policies differ by environment.

**Enforce at creation:** Retroactive tagging projects are painful and incomplete. Printing the owner's name next to every large dataset only works with reliable tags.

**Inside big companies:** The same job is often done with metadata tables listing every file's size, owner, age and last access time. Cloud tags or internal tables, the principle is the same.

quiz.q: You're told to cut storage 20% in a quarter, but half the buckets have no owner tag. Why is that your first problem?
quiz.a: You can't show or charge cost to teams, and nobody can confirm untagged data is safe to delete. Every later step, showback, chargeback, quotas and waste hunting, needs owners.

mcq.q: Which three tags should every bucket, volume and table carry?
options: Owner team, service and environment
Region, storage class and size
Creation date, last access and cost
Project, budget code and approver
mcq.why: Owner, service and environment make cost attributable and let policies like retention differ between production and staging.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
hook: Bill teams for their storage and behavior changes fast. So why do most companies wait to do it?
title: Showback builds awareness; chargeback changes behavior
body: **Showback** reports each team's storage cost to them. **Chargeback** bills it to their budget. Showback builds awareness: teams learn what their data costs. Chargeback changes behavior, because real money leaves their budget. But it needs accurate data, or teams will fight the numbers. So many companies start with showback and switch to chargeback once tagging and cost data are trusted.
takeaway: Show the bill until it's trusted. Then send it.
deeper:
**Why the order:** If a team is charged for data it doesn't own, or at a cost it can't verify, the conversation becomes a dispute about the numbers instead of a decision about the data.

**Showback debugs the data:** It's low stakes. Teams reviewing dashboards spot mis-tagged resources and wrong allocations. Once those are fixed and the numbers are credible, chargeback can switch on.

**Why chargeback works:** It aligns incentives. When a team's own budget pays for its storage, retention, compression and tiering become that team's priorities.

**The playbook view:** Showback, chargeback and quotas are a medium-effort lever with a behavioral, lasting saving and team friction as the main risk. The best first target is all teams, because the goal is cost awareness across the whole organization.

quiz.q: Your company turns on chargeback on day one while tags are 60% complete. What happens in the first month?
quiz.a: Teams get billed for data that isn't theirs or can't verify their charges, so they fight the numbers instead of fixing storage. Showback first would have exposed and fixed the bad tags.

mcq.q: Why do many companies start with showback before chargeback?
options: Cost data must be accurate and trusted before money moves
Cloud billing tools cannot support chargeback
Showback produces larger savings than chargeback
Chargeback only applies to on-prem storage
mcq.why: Chargeback moves real budget, so tags and allocations must be right first. Otherwise teams dispute the numbers.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
hook: Which prefix hasn't been read in a year? Which team owns the most cold data? Who can tell you?
title: S3 Storage Lens and metadata tables find the waste
body: You can't cut what you can't see. AWS **S3 Storage Lens** gives 62 free metrics at bucket level with 14 days of history. Paid advanced metrics add prefix-level views, 15 months of history and organization-wide views across thousands of accounts. Other clouds have similar tools. Inside big companies, **metadata tables** list every file's size, owner, age and last access time, and engineers query them to find waste.
takeaway: Waste hunting becomes a query once last access time is a column.
deeper:
**What they answer:** Which buckets grew most this month, which prefixes haven't been read in a year, which datasets lack lifecycle rules, which teams own the most cold data. This is the Inform phase of FinOps and the find-waste step of the storage flow.

**Free versus paid:** Bucket-level metrics with 14 days show the current state, not trends. Prefix-level views show which part of a bucket is responsible, often necessary when one bucket holds data from many sources. Fifteen months of history shows seasonal patterns and whether optimizations stuck.

**The internal version:** One row per file, with last access time, lets engineers ask for all files owned by team X, larger than 1 TB, not read in 180 days. Guesswork becomes a report.

**The bonus:** The same data supplies the measured access that safe tiering needs.

quiz.q: A shared bucket grew 3 PB last quarter. The free Storage Lens dashboard shows only bucket-level totals with 14 days of history. What do you need to find the cause?
quiz.a: Prefix-level views to see which part of the bucket grew, and longer history, which paid advanced metrics give at 15 months, to see when the growth started.

mcq.q: Why is last access time a valuable column in a storage metadata table?
options: It finds unread data to delete or tier
It tells you which replica to repair first
It sets the object's storage class automatically
It measures write amplification per file
mcq.why: Data nobody reads is the prime candidate for deletion or colder tiers, and the field supplies measured access for safe tiering.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
hook: Most teams learn their storage grew too much when the bill arrives. How do you move that moment earlier?
title: Quotas force the conversation before growth
body: Without limits, cost shows up after the fact. Per-team **quotas** force a conversation before growth, not after. Uber used namespace quotas as part of controlling HDFS small files. The companion practice is **unit cost**: track cost per user, per photo or per TB served, not only total cost. Total cost rises with growth. Unit cost shows whether efficiency is actually improving.
takeaway: Total cost says you're growing. Unit cost says whether you're getting better.
deeper:
**Quotas change timing:** Hitting a quota triggers a request, and the request prompts questions. Is this growth expected? Can old data be deleted first? Is there a cheaper tier? Quotas join showback and chargeback as the practices that keep fixes in place.

**Beyond bytes:** HDFS keeps metadata for every file in memory on its NameNode, so millions of tiny files strain the system. Namespace quotas limit file counts and push teams to consolidate small files.

**Why unit cost:** A growing company's storage bill rises every year, which on its own looks like failure. If cost per user or per photo falls, efficiency is improving. Flat total cost with shrinking usage would hide worsening efficiency.

**The catch:** Pick a unit that tracks the business, or the metric improves while nothing real does.

quiz.q: Storage spend rose 30% this year while users grew 60%. The CFO calls it a failure. Which metric settles it?
quiz.a: Cost per user. It fell about 19% (1.3 / 1.6 ≈ 0.81), so efficiency improved even though total cost rose with growth.

mcq.q: Why did Uber use namespace quotas on HDFS?
options: To control the number of small files
To stop teams from using erasure coding
To cap cross-zone replication traffic
To force hot data onto flash
mcq.why: Namespace quotas limit file counts, which helped Uber control HDFS small files that strain NameNode memory.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
hook: An efficiency program asks hundreds of teams to clean up after themselves. Why is it doomed?
title: Efficiency programs fail on memory, win on defaults
body: A storage efficiency program fails if it depends on each team remembering to clean up. It succeeds when the platform makes the cheap choice the **default**. TTLs required when data is created. Lifecycle rules applied by default. Compaction and retention run centrally. And the owner's name printed next to every large dataset. Good defaults stop waste from accumulating without anyone having to think about it.
takeaway: Make the cheap choice the default and the expensive one the effort.
deeper:
**Why memory fails:** Across hundreds of teams, some will always forget, be too busy or move on. A system that relies on voluntary cleanup piles up waste at the rate of its least careful team.

**Each default kills a waste pile:** Required TTLs stop staging and temp data from living forever. Default lifecycle rules handle non-current versions and tier cooling data. Central compaction and retention, as LinkedIn's OpenHouse does, remove old snapshots and orphan files with no per-team work.

**The name tag:** Showing the owner next to large datasets creates social accountability. It's harder to ignore a 5 PB dataset with your name on it.

**The catch:** The levers work only if applied continuously. Across an organization, the only reliable way to do that is to build them into the platform.

quiz.q: You can fund one of two things: a quarterly email asking teams to clean up, or mandatory TTLs at table creation. Which, and why?
quiz.a: Mandatory TTLs. Reminders depend on every team remembering, so waste piles up at the pace of the least careful team. A default applies to every new table automatically.

mcq.q: Which is a platform default that keeps storage waste down?
options: TTLs required when data is created
A yearly cleanup week for all teams
An email reminder to delete old data
A wiki page listing retention guidelines
mcq.why: Defaults act on every dataset automatically. Reminders and guidelines depend on each team remembering, and some always forget.

hook: A cold archive is almost never read. So where does nearly all of its energy go?
title: Cold data spends its energy just existing
body: Storage energy has two parts. The energy to **keep** data: spinning drives, powered servers, cooling, paid every hour whether anyone reads or not. The energy to **serve** it: reads, rebuilds and **scrubbing** (periodically reading data to check for errors). Cold data is rarely read, so keeping dominates. The biggest energy wins for cold data come from media that uses no power at rest.
takeaway: For cold data, energy is rent, not usage.
deeper:
**Hot versus cold:** Hot data spends real energy serving requests. Cold data spends almost all of it on platters spinning, servers powered and fans running, for bytes nobody may read for months.

**The cold-storage levers:** Denser drives put more TB behind each watt. Powering down drives not in use cuts draw at rest. Tape and glass draw no power while stored.

**Cost levers are energy levers:** Every byte deleted, compressed or erasure-coded instead of replicated is a byte no drive has to spin for. Moving from 3× replication to 1.4× erasure coding cuts the energy to keep that data by more than half, just as it cuts hardware.

**The design rule:** Cost efficiency and energy efficiency point the same way.

quiz.q: You must cut energy for a 100 PB archive read a few times a year. Would faster CPUs in the storage servers help much? What would?
quiz.a: Barely: serving is a tiny share for rarely read data. Cutting power at rest helps: denser drives, spinning drives down, or tape, plus deleting or erasure-coding bytes.

mcq.q: For cold data, which part of storage energy dominates?
options: Keeping data: spinning drives, servers and cooling
Serving reads to users
Rebuilding data after failures
Scrubbing data to detect errors
mcq.why: Cold data is rarely read, so power drawn at rest for drives, servers and cooling dwarfs the energy spent serving it.

hook: Meta built cold-storage datacenters on hard drives that drew a fraction of normal power. How?

predict.q: Meta's cold storage racks used about what share of the power of normal storage servers?
options: About one-quarter
About three-quarters
About one-half

title: Meta's cold storage used under one-sixth normal power
body: Meta's cold storage datacenters used less than one-sixth of the power of a normal Meta datacenter. Its cold storage racks used about one-quarter of the power of normal storage servers, because only **one drive per tray** spun at a time. Other media go further. **Tape** uses no power while a cartridge sits in its slot. Microsoft Research's **Project Silica** stores data in glass that needs no power at rest and no periodic refresh. It is still research.
takeaway: The coldest data should cost almost nothing while it sleeps.
deeper:
**Meta's trade:** Keeping one drive per tray spinning accepts slower access, since reading a sleeping drive means waiting for it to spin up, in exchange for a large power cut. For data that is rarely read, that wait is acceptable.

**Tape's extreme:** Cartridges sit unpowered in a library, and a robot loads one into a drive only when needed. Retrieval takes much longer; energy at rest is zero.

**Silica's other angle:** Magnetic media, disk and tape, need scrubbing, periodic reads to detect degradation, and eventually migration to fresh media. Glass needs no periodic refresh and removes the energy spent scrubbing. As research, it isn't a lever you can deploy today.

**The common thread:** All three trade access speed for energy, which suits truly cold data.

quiz.q: A team proposes Meta-style cold racks, one drive per tray spinning, for a photo tier users scroll back to daily. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: Reads often hit sleeping drives and wait for spin-up, so photos that should load in milliseconds come back slowly. The design only suits data that is truly rarely read.

mcq.q: How did Meta's cold storage racks cut power to about a quarter of normal storage servers?
options: Only one drive per tray spun at a time
They stored data on glass instead of disks
They used SSDs instead of hard drives
They ran servers without any cooling
mcq.why: Keeping most drives powered down trades slower access for much lower power, which is acceptable for rarely read data.

hook: Swap 4 TB drives for 24 TB drives in a cold tier. What happens to energy per terabyte?

predict.q: Assuming 8 W per spinning drive, how does energy per TB change from 4 TB to 24 TB drives?
options: About 6× lower
About the same
About 2× lower

title: At an assumed 8 W, a 24 TB drive uses 6× less per TB
body: A back-of-envelope with one assumption: every hard drive uses about **8 watts** while spinning. A 4 TB drive then uses 2 watts per TB. A 24 TB drive uses about 0.33 watts per TB. Denser drives cut energy per TB about 6 times, before counting server and cooling savings. That is one more reason to fill cold tiers with the biggest drives, and to move truly cold data to media that can be powered off.
takeaway: The density that hurts hot data's IOPS is pure gain for cold data's power.
deeper:
**Same physics, two effects:** A drive's power, like its IOPS, comes mostly from its motor and arm, not its capacity. As capacity grows, both IOPS per TB and watts per TB fall. For hot data, falling IOPS per TB is a problem. For cold data, falling watts per TB is pure benefit.

**It compounds:** Fewer drives for the same data means fewer servers, fewer racks and less cooling. The 6× figure is before counting any of that.

**Where it points:** Cold, capacity-bound data belongs on the densest drives for cost and energy alike. Data colder still should move to tape or other media that can be powered off.

**The broader win:** Deleting and compressing data are sustainability wins too. Energy per TB falls with denser drives and powered-off media.

quiz.q: Using the 8 W assumption, how many watts does storing 240 TB take on 4 TB drives versus 24 TB drives, counting drives only?
quiz.a: 4 TB drives: 60 drives × 8 W = 480 W. 24 TB drives: 10 drives × 8 W = 80 W. Six times less, before servers and cooling.

mcq.q: Why do denser drives cut energy per TB for cold data?
options: Drive power barely depends on capacity, so watts spread over more TB
Denser drives spin more slowly than smaller ones
Larger drives need less cooling per drive
Denser drives power off automatically when idle
mcq.why: At an assumed 8 W per drive, 24 TB gives about 0.33 W per TB versus 2 W per TB at 4 TB.

hook: Three cost levers need no new hardware and little engineering. Which should you pull first?
title: Start with deletion, tiering and compression
body: Rank levers by saving, effort and risk, and three come first. **Deleting unused data** and adding TTLs: high but variable saving, low to medium effort, risk of deleting needed data; start with temp, staging and old snapshots. **Lifecycle tiering**: often more than half of storage cost for cold data, low effort, risks of retrieval fees and minimum durations; start with logs, old media, backups. **Compression**: 10% to 15% over zlib, more with columnar, low effort, CPU risk.
takeaway: Pull the levers with the shortest payback first.
deeper:
**Two kinds of tiering:** Lifecycle tiering moves objects on fixed rules, such as after 90 days. Access-based tiering, like S3 Intelligent-Tiering, moves objects by observed access: similar savings, no retrieval fees, very low effort. Its risks are a monitoring fee and ignoring small objects; it suits mixed or unknown access.

**Compression targets:** Logs and lake tables. They are large, compressible and often stored in formats that can switch codecs or move to columnar layout.

**Why start here:** Payback. These levers need no hardware and little engineering, so payback is short. Under 3 months is an easy yes, and these are the likeliest to clear it.

**The risks are manageable:** Verify data is truly unneeded before deleting. Model retrieval fees and object sizes before tiering. Choose compression levels by data temperature.

quiz.q: A bucket holds data with no known access pattern: some objects are hot, some untouched for years. Which tiering approach fits, and what's the trade-off?
quiz.a: Access-based tiering such as S3 Intelligent-Tiering. It moves objects by observed use without retrieval fees, but charges a monitoring fee and ignores small objects.

mcq.q: What are the playbook's listed risks for lifecycle tiering?
options: Retrieval fees and minimum storage durations
Deleting data someone still needs
Garbage collection bugs that lose data
Rebuild network and CPU load
mcq.why: Moving data to cool classes adds per-GB fees when it's read and bills a minimum period even if it's deleted early.

hook: Erasure coding, SMR and dedup can save a lot. Why aren't they where you start?
title: Platform-scale levers save big but need real engineering
body: Some levers save a lot but change how the platform behaves. **Erasure coding** instead of 3× replication: overhead from 3× to 1.33× to 1.67×, high effort, rebuild network and CPU as the risk; best for large sealed files. Denser drives and SMR: more than 20% at Dropbox, high effort, falling IOPS per TB as the risk; best for cold, sequential blobs. Deduplication: saving depends on duplicate rate, medium effort, GC bugs can lose data.
takeaway: The biggest savings change how data survives, so they need the most testing.
deeper:
**The middle of the table:** Compaction merges small files into large ones: fewer requests and better compression, at the risk of write amplification, the extra writes from rewriting data. Best target: streaming lake tables. Right-sizing replicas removes one copy's cost per extra replica at low effort, with lower durability as the risk; best on duplicate disaster-recovery and lake copies. Dedup's best targets are backups and shared attachments.

**Why the effort:** These levers touch correctness or performance. Erasure coding changes how data survives failures. SMR changes write patterns. Dedup changes deletion. Compaction rewrites live data. Each needs careful engineering and testing, and the payback period must include that time.

**Who uses them:** They are the levers behind the big industry case studies: f4 and Tectonic for erasure coding, Dropbox for SMR. At exabyte scale the effort pays many times over.

quiz.q: A 200 TB startup wants to build its own erasure coding layer to save money. What would you suggest instead, and why?
quiz.a: Start with deletion, tiering and compression. Erasure coding is high-effort platform work with rebuild network and CPU risk; its payback is compelling at exabyte scale, not at 200 TB.

mcq.q: What is the playbook's listed risk for deduplication?
options: GC bugs can lose data
IOPS per TB drops
Rebuild network and CPU load
Lower zone isolation
mcq.why: Dedup deletes a chunk only when no references remain, so a reference-counting or GC bug can remove data others still need.

hook: The last three levers in the cost playbook don't touch a single stored byte. What do they target?
title: Traffic and behavior levers finish the job
body: The last levers target traffic and people. **Reducing egress with a CDN**: large savings for media, medium effort, cache misses as the risk; best for photos and videos. **Avoiding cross-zone chatter**: can save more than the disk cost, medium effort, lower zone isolation as the risk; best for self-managed replicated databases. **Showback, chargeback and quotas**: behavioral, lasting savings, medium effort, team friction as the risk; they apply to all teams.
takeaway: Technical levers fix today's bytes. Behavioral levers fix tomorrow's.
deeper:
**The overlooked lines:** Egress and cross-zone traffic don't show up as storage in most engineers' mental models. Yet each can dominate the right workload: egress for a video streaming service, cross-zone transfer for a write-heavy self-managed database.

**Why behavior lasts:** Showback and quotas don't remove bytes directly. They make teams care about bytes, so the other levers get applied continuously. The saving lasts because it changes how data is created and kept.

**The whole playbook in one pass:**
1. Understand the true cost of a usable TB.
2. Read the bill line by line.
3. Pull fewer-bytes and cheaper-bytes levers where payback is shortest.
4. Consider owning only at large, steady scale.
5. Run it as continuous FinOps with good defaults.

**The bonus:** Every lever that removes bytes also saves energy.

quiz.q: A self-managed database across three zones spends more on transfer than on disk. Which lever applies, and what do you give up?
quiz.a: Avoid cross-zone chatter, for example by keeping replicas in fewer zones. The saving can exceed disk cost, but you give up zone isolation, so one zone outage hurts more.

mcq.q: What is the playbook's main risk for reducing egress with a CDN?
options: Cache misses
Team friction
Lower zone isolation
Minimum storage durations
mcq.why: Only cache misses go back to the origin, so a poor hit rate brings back origin egress and GET charges.
